#167. Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

China thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

#168. Rivian buys world model startup to accelerate self-driving ambitions

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

EV maker Rivian has acquired Third Dimension, a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds.

Rivian isn’t getting into gaming, but it does want to leverage Third Dimension’s technology to turn real-world data into 3D worlds that can accelerate the development of its advanced driver-assistance features and the self-driving system for the robotaxis it plans to supply to Uber.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The 15-person team at Third Dimension, most of whom are based in the U.K., will be absorbed into Rivian’s autonomy and AI team led by James Philbin. The acquisition also gives Rivian an opportunity to expand its AI hub in London, Philbin said in an exclusive interview.

Third Dimension, which was founded by CEO Tolga Kart and Piotr Sokólski in 2024, raised $7 million in seed funding from venture capital firms, including Abstract Ventures, MVP, Soma Capital, and Solari Capital. While the company’s technology was built to speed up video game development, the founders saw other potential applications, including defense and autonomous vehicles.

Now, under Rivian, they’ll be focused on automated driving. Today, Rivian offers “Universal Hands-Free” driving software that lets drivers take their hands off the wheel on highways, while still watching the road. The company plans to, by the end of the year, release a version of the software that can handle the entire drive through surface streets and highways without touching the wheel, although the driver will still have to supervise and be ready to take over.

Rivian is also working toward full autonomy, which it will deploy in the robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on the Uber app in 2028.

“The team is excited to be able to focus on one problem,” Kart told TechCrunch in an interview. “I think as a small company, having to serve many, many different masters is very hard, and so we’re very excited to come work on a problem that has such an amount of scale, where our technology makes a true difference.”

Simulation is a critical tool for autonomous vehicle developers, who use it to train and validate self-driving systems. Historically, these simulators were built on rendering or video game engines and often relied on synthetic data. These virtual environments might look like the real world, but a gap between the two remains, Kart said. The workaround typically requires feeding the simulators ever-larger amounts of data in hopes of closing that quality gap.

Third Dimension’s technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian’s reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator.

“For us, it’s about taking real scenarios, but making them simulatable,” Philbin said. “These are not synthetic kind of video game styles, they’re real things that happen in the world, but now we get that extra dial of being able to move the cameras around, shift other agents, have maybe different lighting or weather conditions. So it’s a really powerful tool for us.”

It’s technology that Philbin said the company knew it wanted and had actually “done a pretty extensive kind of evaluation of a lot of different providers.”

Any company developing automated driving technology needs data — and a lot of it. But the quality matters too. Real-world data collected from cameras and other sensors is especially valuable.

Rivian collects driving data from tens of thousands of R1T pickup trucks, R1S SUVs, delivery vans, and R2 SUVs on the road today — essentially any vehicle whose owner has enabled external camera sharing. Rivian uses that data, which is aggregated and anonymized, to build training models for driving. According to Philbin, Rivian gets more than 400,000 sequences uploaded from its customer fleets per day.

Third Dimension’s tech will allow Rivian to simulate complex driving conditions without having to wait for rare real-world edge cases to occur, Philbin said.

“Especially when you think about validation, right? So that’s really the piece where you’re saying, ‘is the system good to ship?’” Philbin said. “And there, you really want to have a good sense of this sim-to-real gap, because to do that kind of hand on heart, you really need to trust that answer is in the positive. Otherwise, you’re measuring something that’s not representative of how it will actually perform in the real world.”

This article was updated to include more quotes from Philbin and more details on Rivian’s automated driving strategy.

#173. France: 1 killed, 4 wounded after shooting near Paris

French police arrested a suspect after gunshots were fired on the outskirts of Paris in what President Macron described as a racist and terrorist attack.

One person was killed and four others were injured when gunshots were fired from a vehicle outside Paris on Friday, according to local authorities.

Interior Minister ⁠Laurent ​Nunez said the shooting was "clearly a terrorist crime."

He said shots were fired at the total of three locations in the towns of Trappes and La Verriere, which are located about 20 kilometers (13 miles) west of the French capital, close to Versailles. The "rampage" lasted for 15 minutes, according to the minister.

Nunez said the shooter fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon."

Three of the wounded remain in critical condition.

Commenting on the shooting, President Emmanuel Macron said the attack "marks a ⁠turning ​point" for France.

"What ‌happened today was a terrorist ​and ⁠racist attack," he told reporters, noting that the victims were targeted due to their religion and the color of their skin.

Shortly after the Friday attack, authorities detained a man in the neighboring town of Coignieres and took him into police custody.

The authorities later identified the suspect as Kevin T., born in 1987. They said the alleged shooter already had a criminal record.

France's anti-terrorism prosecutor said the authorities found a Sten Gun — a British-made WWII-era submachine gun — and a tear gas grenade in his car.  The alleged shooter had also booby-trapped his apartment, according to the authorities.

"An individual fired shots from his vehicle at multiple people along his route," the mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, wrote on social media.

He later told French broadcaster BFM TV that one of the locations at which shots were fired was a playground.

"It is a miracle that there were not more victims," he said.

Rabeh said the person killed was of African origin, while one of those critically wounded was of North African origin.

The mayor also told reporters the attack had "racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."

“This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism,” he said.

Aurore Berge, the French minister in charge of gender equality and antidiscrimination, said a 12-year-old girl was very seriously injured in the incident.

"If a racist motive is established, I hope that the whole nation will stand alongside the residents of Trappes, La Verriere, and the victims. We cannot tolerate even the slightest racist remark in the French republic," she said.

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the incident "very serious" and said that "all available resources of the security forces and judicial authorities have been fully mobilized."

He added that France's National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office (Pnat) is monitoring the situation.

Pnat itself said it had opened an investigation into "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, with the aggravating circumstance that the acts were committed on the basis of the victim's actual or perceived membership of a specific race, ethnicity, nation or religion."

The shooting came as France braces for yet another day of protests against the high cost of living on Saturday, with major museums in Paris and other major cities closing their doors and the government deploying a significantly larger security presence.

"We are not talking about ​a nice protest," Interior Minister Nunez told reporters, announcing the deployment of 70,000 security personnel. "We are ​ready ⁠tomorrow to be extremely firm ⁠and ​not tolerate anything."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

France has also seen a spate of Islamist terrorist attacks in recent years and, although the number of incidents has fallen, authorities have warned that risks remain.

The town of Trappes has experienced its own share of tension, with a local teacher reporting receiving threats after saying that the state did not do enough to protect Samuel Paty, a teacher in another Paris suburb who was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Mohammed.

There was no immediate suggestion that Friday's shooting was linked either to the current protests or Islamist terrorism.

#175. Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worse

High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment can be added to the federal treasurer’s wall of worries

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Jim Chalmers in a speech last week offered the scant encouragement that the economy would be “a bit better” in a year’s time.

Fast forward to Friday morning, and the treasurer revealed that his officials were busy downgrading their forecasts ahead of December’s mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment.

In other words, things are getting worse, not better.

Overnight, a broadening Middle East conflict pushed the global benchmark oil price to US$113, and within sight of its April high of nearly US$120.

Motorists are paying 60 cents more for a litre of petrol prices than they were before the US and Israel attacked Iran. That’s an extra $36 to fill up a 60-litre tank. Do that once a week and a family’s monthly fuel bill is $144 higher than in February.

The New York Times overnight reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to restart attacks on Iran after the upcoming American midterm elections.

Westpac analysts have sketched out an “escalation” scenario for the Middle East conflict where oil climbs towards US$150, echoing warnings from the International Monetary Fund earlier this month.

That worst-case scenario would have huge implications for inflation and interest rates, even as we brace for a potential fifth interest rate hike on 3 November.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Meanwhile, the one bright spot that has helped paper over many of the cracks in the global economy – the huge spending associated with artificial intelligence – has hit some serious wobbles.

Investors are worried about the huge surge in debt among companies racing to build the infrastructure for an AI future – the trigger for another steep sell-off on Wall Street overnight.

Community opposition to the massive datacentre build-out could stall the headlong rush towards an AI future. That is likely a good thing in the longer term, but in the short term is another stress to add to the wall of worries. Rising chatter of a new tech stock bubble is naturally accompanied by talk of an imminent bust.

With all this going on, no wonder that the treasurer can only offer the thinnest of gruel for Australians hungry for any evidence of an end to years of disruption, and of wages that can’t keep up with high and rising prices.

High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment is a central banker’s “nightmare”, as the Reserve Bank’s Andrew Hauser has said.

It’s also a nightmare for a federal treasurer who is increasingly unpopular and desperate for a win in the court of public opinion.

“The pressures on people right now are very substantial and obviously that keeps me awake at night,” Chalmers told Politico.

“And there’s a number of reasons for that, some of them are outside our control, and some of them we have some influence over. You know, providing some cost-of-living help, managing the budget in a responsible way,” he said.

Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you

“Those are the things that we can do, but in lots of ways we’re hostage as well to decisions taken in DC or Tehran or in Eastern Europe about two wars which are pushing up inflation around the world and weighing on growth around the world.”

The high level of government spending is not helping the inflation fight, by any means – something the opposition is keen to point out at every opportunity.

Productivity growth is, if not dead, then resting, and shows no signs of springing back to its perch. That means more inflation at lower rates of growth as the economy hits its speed limits sooner.

But Chalmers is right when he says there’s a lot that is out of the government’s control.

His options to alleviate voter discontent are limited, which is why he frequently falls back on platitudes and lines to the effect of “you think we have it bad? You should see other economies.”

Sure, the government can lower petrol prices through another temporary cut to the fuel excise. But the billions of dollars that pumps into motorists’ pockets makes it harder for the RBA to bring inflation back under control.

Labor could go the other way and announce plans for big spending cuts in the December mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.

That would help the central bank’s job, but would drag on an already weak economy and push unemployment higher – would they win any plaudits for that?

This is Hauser’s “world of hard choices” – a world where the solution to one problem makes the other worse. A world with which Australians are becoming all too familiar.

Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editor

#176. Arc browser sunsets December 22 as The Browser Company doubles down on Dia

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

The Browser Company is sunsetting its design-forward Arc browser on December 22, 2026, and directing users to Dia, its AI-first browser. The company announced the decision on Thursday, citing the rising cost of keeping a browser secure in the age of AI.

“Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI,” the company wrote.

“Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.”

The wind-down is staged into three parts. As of Thursday, new Arc accounts can no longer be created. On November 23, Arc Search on iOS and Android will lose its AI features, including “Browse for Me.” Users will no longer be able to sign in or sync tabs, though the app will continue functioning as a basic local browser.

On December 22, Arc will stop working entirely on Mac and Windows. Accounts will be deactivated, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days. Arc Search will also be removed from the Google Play Store.

While The Browser Company claims Dia now surpasses Arc in speed, stability, and security benchmarks, user reactions on social media were largely disappointed, with many reviving requests for the company to make Arc open source.

But CEO Josh Miller previously pointed out that Arc is built on the Arc Development Kit (ADK) — a proprietary internal SDK that is also the core engine powering Dia. Open-sourcing Arc would mean giving away Dia’s intellectual property.

“While we’d love to open-source Arc someday, we can’t do that meaningfully without also open-sourcing ADK,” Miller previously noted. “And ADK is still core to our company’s value.”

For users making the switch, Dia will carry over equivalents of several core Arc features. Users can still swipe between different work and personal environments using Dia’s “Profiles” (formerly Arc’s Spaces). Arc’s signature vertical tabs will remain as an optional sidebar layout, while Folders have been rebranded as “Pinned Tab Groups.”

Passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history will seamlessly transfer to Dia. Arc features will remain free in Dia, with AI optional.

The shutdown officially closes a chapter that began in 2025, when the startup stopped active feature development on Arc. The Browser Company — which was acquired by Atlassian for $610 million in 2025 — conceded at the time that while early adopters loved the browser’s novel interface, the “novelty tax” and complexity limited mainstream adoption. Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned.

#183. Sri Lanka: Death of iconic elephant raises habitat concerns

The death of what was thought to be Sri Lanka’s largest elephant has drawn attention to human-elephant conflict in rural communities. The island country sees a high number of deadly encounters.

The recent death of an iconic male elephant in Sri Lanka has raised concerns over ongoing contact between humans and the giant animals, whose habitats have been greatly reduced.

The elephant known as "Kavantissa" had been considered to be the tallest living male elephant in the Sri Lanka. Thought to be around 45 years old and measuring roughly 3.3 meters tall (11 feet), he roamed Sri Lanka's northwest near the village of Galgamuwa, and was widely admired for his majestic stature.

In late September, villagers noticed the 5.5 ton-tusker (5,500 kg) was limping, and a closer look reveled a gunshot wound on his right leg. Despite the intervention of veterinary surgeons, the elephant died on October 16.

Sri Lanka records the highest number of elephant deaths annually and the second highest number of human deaths globally from violent interactions between elephants and humans, which usually happen when crop raiding elephants encroach on farmlands.

According to official statistics, since 2019, an average of 370 elephants and 125 humans have died in human-elephant conflict incidents each year.

The situation affects the natural habitats of elephants and the livelihoods of rural communities.

Home to about 10% of the global Asian elephant population and occupying about 2% of their total natural range, Sri Lanka has the highest density of Asian elephants in the world.

The Sri Lankan elephant is an endangered subspecies in the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species, and protected under Sri Lankan law, with punishment by fines and jail terms for wildlife-related offences.

During the past few decades, forest cover in Sri Lanka has shrunk as the population has grown.

Statistics show the rural population of Sri Lanka increased from 8.25 million in 1960 to 17.8 million in 2020.

Agriculture remains the primary source of income for these rural communities. As a result, the land is cleared for agricultural activities.

According to Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) statistics, in 2024, an estimated 7,451 wild elephants were recorded in Sri Lanka. About 70% of these wild elephants live outside protected areas.

Research shows elephants have a massive daily dietary requirement of about 150 kilograms (330 lbs.) of green matter, which drives them into farmland.

"Driven primarily by habitat loss, agricultural expansion, fragmentation of elephant corridors, and increasing competition for land and resources, human-elephant conflict continues to cause hundreds of elephant deaths and more than 100 human fatalities annually," said Ravi Corea, President of Sri Lanka Wildlife Conservation Society, a Sri Lankan non-profit conservation organization.

The conservationist told DW that rural communities are severely affected, and the agricultural losses caused by elephants can threaten a family's primary source of food and income.

"This distinguishes human-elephant conflict from many human-wildlife conflicts in economically developed countries, where wildlife encounters, although sometimes serious, generally do not threaten household subsistence to the same extent," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Despite the efforts by the government to mitigate HEC, the numbers are rising demonstrating the continuing severity of the crisis," Corea added.

Elephants are shot, poisoned, or killed by improvised explosives hidden in food and train collisions, experts say.

In view of the escalation of human-elephant conflict, the Sri Lankan government in 2020 drafted a national action plan to mitigate the problem.

"The 2020 Action Plan provides a valuable foundation for reducing human–elephant conflict, but its recommendations must be strengthened through a comprehensive national conservation strategy with enforceable habitat protection at its core,"  Corea said.

"The ultimate measure of success must be not merely a reduction in human–elephant conflict, but the permanent protection of ecologically connected habitats, the survival of viable wild elephant populations and the ability of people and elephants to coexist sustainably for generations to come," he added.

Meanwhile, community-based programs by non-government organizations have proven effective and sustainable. These initiatives are complemented by elephant monitoring, scientific research, habitat assessments, community education, and the development of locally appropriate deterrents, Corea said

"Our flagship initiative Project Orange Elephant in Sri Lanka's Wasgamuwa region promotes the cultivation of citrus which elephants do not like to eat as a trophic deterrence. This reduces crop raiding while generating alternative income for farmers," Corea added, pointing to things like electric fencing protecting settlements and agricultural lands while encouraging local responsibility.

Another issue is confrontations on elephant corridors, that in some cases have discouraged children from walking to school.

Elephant corridors are designated strips of land that connect larger forest and habitat patches, allowing elephants to move safely between them for food, water, breeding, and seasonal migration.

To address this, the "EleFriendly" bus service in Wasgamuwa, provides safe transportation for schoolchildren through elephant corridors and has reduced dangerous human-elephant encounters along its original route by over 90%.

"An ethically just solution must protect human lives, livelihoods, and elephant populations simultaneously, said Kamal Shashendra, a Sri Lanka-based environmental ethics researcher.

He told DW that this required scientifically informed land-use planning, protection of elephant corridors, appropriate community-based fencing, effective early-warning systems, and fair compensation for affected families.

He said: “Don’t let this terrorist attack divide us.” He called for “respect and unity”, saying many French people would be scared and thinking “this could happen to me”.

Ali Rabeh, the leftwing mayor of Trappes, said the gunman had set out by car on Friday morning “firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath” as he drove through the town and neighbouring La Verrière. The mayor called it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.

Rabeh, whose family has Moroccan roots, said: “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.

“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country. Her crime was probably being of colour,” he added. “It’s probably one of the first attempts at a mass crime of Islamophobia and racism.”

Rabeh said everyone in France had a responsibility to bring “calm and harmony”. He called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.

Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether the gunman targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.

The 39-year-old suspect, who was stopped by police in his car, was named by France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor as Kevin T. He had driven through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière in Yvelines at about 10.30am on Friday. Over the course of 15 minutes, he repeatedly fired an automatic weapon, first at a petrol station, then a medical centre and a children’s playground.

The French public broadcaster reported that he shot dead a young black man, then targeted a woman wearing a headscarf, before shooting the 12-year-old girl, who was being treated for her eight gunshot wounds at a children’s hospital on Friday night.

The prosecutor said in a statement on Friday night that the medical status of the five wounded victims was not stable.

The man killed was named as Pengo Bossio Wangi in an Instagram post by the mixed martial arts academy of which he was a member. The Atch Academy paid tribute to a man who “set an example” and said that memories of “his smile, his energy, and his generosity will remain etched within our walls and in our hearts”.

Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of La Verrière, told Agence France-Presse that two of the wounded people in his town were cleaners of African origin attending to a school Friday on morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire.

The prosecutor said that when the suspect was stopped by police in his car he was found with a sten gun – a British submachine gun used in the second world war – as well as teargas grenades.

The man had also booby-trapped his home with gas canisters and electric wires connected to a timer, authorities said, adding that a member of his family was arrested and taken into custody for questioning.

A student at a rally for President Lula da Silva

In the sprawling former industrial city of Osasco, shuttered factories have given way to a shopping malls and delivery app tech companies in what is now dubbed SÃ£o Paulo's "Silicon Valley."

The municipality voted for Brazil's left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva in 2022 but switched to the right-wing FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro in the first round of Brazil's presidential election this month. Bolsonaro won that vote - and now the two men face a run-off on Sunday. Since 1989, every first-round winner has gone on to be elected president.

Like many of President Lula's traditional supporters, Gilberto Almazan, who leads a metalworkers' union here, is visibly worried.

He cries when he tells Lula's life story: a boy who grew up in hunger in the north-east, who became a metalworker, then a union leader, then a three-time president. But he's candid about how things have changed here and how the union movement that was so integral to Lula's support base is stuck in the "Middle Ages", and struggling to keep up.

"We had strong deindustrialisation here," Almazan says. "The profile of the working class changed. They are no longer predominantly industrial workers, they are service workers.

"Metal, chemical, textile factories disappeared. And five malls were built."

The word "change" comes up repeatedly among Bolsonaro supporters here. Many struggle to name specific Bolsonaro policies they like but know they want to try something different: frustrated by the economy, crime and corruption in politics â even though FlÃ¡vio has been faced accusations of corruption too, which he denies.

Tairine says high prices are a problem for her

"He brings the hope of change, that we can have a different Brazil," says lawyer Gisele Bonfim in Osasco, who decided to vote for Bolsonaro after supporting Lula in 2022.

Lula's re-election campaign has been hampered by voters turning away from him. In some cases, their frustration drove abstention, which was higher than average this year, but others like Gisele actively wanted something new.

One major reason for that is Brazil's working class has transformed seismically in places like Osasco.

Near one large shopping mall lies an open-air market where this shift is noticeable. Everyone is touting products, armed with a portable card machine.

Tairine, who sells hot dogs, used to abstain from voting, even though - as voting is compulsory in Brazil - not going to the polls incurs a fine. This year, she plans to vote for Bolsonaro. She points to high taxes paid on "everything" she buys and says these make it "so difficult for a poor person" dealing with inflation, arguing "nothing has changed" since Lula became president again.

FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro has proposed cutting government spending, government ministries, and some taxes - though he has said he'd maintain some of Lula's flagship welfare programmes.

For his supporters, Lula is a working-class hero credited with advancing workers' rights through organising strikes and lifting millions of people out of poverty with generous social welfare programmes as president.

But across Brazil millions now work in the gig economy, a phenomenon Almazan calls "Uber-isation": driving for Uber, delivering food, or running small businesses from market stalls to providing at-home beauty treatments.

"There are a lot of workers who need more freedom, flexibility of days and hours," he says, rather than the welfare and collective action Lula offered.

Robson used to support Lula but has since switched to support Bolsonaro

Richard Lapper, who has written biographies of both Lula and Jair Bolsonaro â Flavio's father who was president from 2019-2022 - says the rise of individualised work and the decline of manufacturing caused by globalisation are not unique to Brazil. But because Brazil industrialised late and deindustrialised early, he argues, the effects have been sharper here. He calls Lula a "victim of his own success."

Unemployment fell to a record low, and Brazil was taken off the United Nation's Hunger Map during Lula's current presidency. But Lapper describes a crisis of "expectations" where people are now better off but don't feel it because prices have risen and household debt and interest rates are high.

Robson, 53, is a municipal civil servant in Osasco. Originally from Lula's north-eastern home state of Pernambuco, he grew up supporting him.

But he describes a country now running deficits and says its citizens are enduring the "worst phase" of its tax burden, which he blames on the Lula government's "mismanagement" of the economy and high public spending.

"Now you have to make choices: pay an instalment for your car, or put food on the table," he says.

In some areas, Lula lost votes compared to 2022, even though Bolsonaro did not gain more than his father did then: 33 million people did not vote in the first round, the highest abstention since 1998.

In response, Lula's campaign has focused on mobilising hundreds of thousands of people â particularly students â on to the streets to get the vote out for round two. It claims one rally in SÃ£o Paulo attracted about a million people.

"A lot of people didn't vote, they thought it wouldn't change anything," says one supporter, Leila. "Our fight is to make those people believe their vote changes things."

Aerial videos of these huge demonstrations have been plastered across social media. An image of a topless man with a six-pack waving a Lula flag at one has been shared tens of millions of times.

The strategy is that their revolution will not be televised, but it should ideally go viral.

Lula, 80, has also been using social media to dismiss criticisms that he is past his prime: calling himself the "king of selfies" and posting videos showing him running from A to B on the campaign trail.

Some people who live in the favelas fear security forces entering if Bolsonaro is elected

In MarÃ©, one of Rio's largest favelas which is controlled by rival gangs, abstention was higher than average.

This dented Lula's support, even though he still won here: among Brazil's very poorest, Lula's welfare initiatives clearly do still resonate. One 18-year-old mother in MarÃ©, Vitoria, earns less than Â£300 a month and praises Lula's government for increasing the minimum wage, giving workers the right to two days off, and providing essential medicines for free.

She is sceptical of Bolsonaro's plans to designate the gang which controls this part of the favela, Comando Vermelho, as a terrorist organisation, which he lobbied the US to do earlier this year.

She thinks it will lead to authorities entering the favela to "kill, destroy, ruin families, leave blood and bodies on the ground", citing a police raid in Rio last year that killed more than 130 people.

Another resident, Andreza DionÃ­sio, blames high abstention rates here on both last-minute changes to polling station locations, but also "a sense of hopelessness about the future."

Many Brazilians now worship in evangelical churches like the Assembleia de Deus VitÃ³ria em Cristo

Increasingly, that void of hope is being filled by the growth of the evangelical church: about a quarter of Brazilians are now evangelical. Its mega-churches offer not just a spiritual home but support with issues like childcare, employment advice and even food.

Its conservative pastors are some of Brazil's most powerful political operators.

Silas Malafaia, who has millions of followers on social media, leads the Assembleia de Deus VitÃ³ria em Cristo headquartered in the lower middle-class neighbourhood of Penha in Rio de Janeiro. He is being investigated for allegedly obstructing the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro, which he denies and calls politically motivated.

At one two-hour sermon he preaches messages of self-improvement to an emotional crowd of hundreds, interrupted occasionally for live music interludes and breaks to collect money with card machines. The whole event is live-streamed on YouTube.

Afterwards, in his office adorned with a photo of him and the former president Jair Bolsonaro, at whose wedding he officiated, he told the BBC that without the evangelical church in working-class neighbourhoods the country would be "in a state worse than you can imagine".

"It gives these people meaning. To better their lives."

Pastor Silas Malafaia officiated at Jair Bolsonaro's wedding

He argues FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro shares the church's values: for family, and against gender "ideology" and abortion.

The church is driving some to actively vote for FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, but among much of Brazil's new working class, the first round feels more like a rejection of President Lula than an endorsement of his rival.

"There will never be another Lula," Gilberto Almazan fears. He intends this as a compliment, but Brazil's changing world of work means it's also probably true.

While Lula's past story still stirs great emotion for people like Almazan, his political fate may depend on whether voters think he can now offer Brazil a new one.

#193. Greece joins countries putting age-limits on social media, banning access for kids under 15

Greece has passed legislation banning social media access for children under 15. New rules will come into effect on January 1, 2027, and are designed to protect children's mental health.

A bill to "ban the use of online social media services by minors" was passed by a majority vote of the Greek parliament Thursday and will go into effect on January 1, 2027.

The New Democracy party was the only bloc in parliament to support the measure; while opposition parties SYRIZA, Greek Solution, KKE, Niki and Freedom Course voted against it, and PASOK abstained.

Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Dimitris Papastergiou called the step, "necessary, effective, proportionate and EU-law-compliant," according to Greek newspaper Kathimerini, adding that social media platforms would have until the first of the year to, "determine whether the accounts they host and the services they provide are intended for adults or not."

Pointing to similar age limits on alcohol and tobacco sales to minors, Papastergiou said lawmakers had no time to wait for Brussels to pass "the perfect European law," saying, "let's send the message that the problem of uncontrolled internet use — which leads children to addiction at the expense of their mental health — cannot continue."

The move to put legal age limits on social media use began last year in Australia, with numerous countries around the world swiftly following suit.

Greece is one of seven EU countries seeking to introduce standards for age-verification on social media, which proponents argue will curb the "endless scrolling" that deprives kids of sleep, destroys their attention span and ability to concentrate and keeps them from playing outdoors and spending time with their friends.

Papastergiou defended the use of an app known as "Kid's Wallet" as a means to that end, saying that it had been established according to codes and technical specifications set by the EU.

The minister was emphatic that the app, "does not provide any personal data whatsoever about children or users, other than whether they are over or under 15 years of age — not even their date of birth."

"We owe our children their childhood," said Papastergiou. "That is what we are doing today. We have a duty to protect them. Given the current challenges, the social media bill delivers what society has been waiting for."

Residents in Oleshky have been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis due to the lack of food, electricity and other resources

The White House has issued a statement saying Melania Trump has helped broker a ‘ceasefire’ in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where residents have been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis due to the lack of food, electricity and other resources.

The small town in southern Kherson has been the centre of an increasingly desperate humanitarian crisis under Russian occupation.

Since May, Russia has failed to deliver food, medicine or other essential goods to the area leading to deaths from starvation and disease. #196. Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests

A town in mourning: One week after protests left historic French town hall in ruins

"It is a historical tragedy for France, not just Limoges".

Just six months into his mayoral term, it is hard to imagine Guillaume GuÃ©rin having a more momentous week.

We talk next to what became the defining image of last week's nationwide protests: the still impressive, yet fragile exterior of his town's 19th-Century town hall, charred from a fire.

The sight of its wooden clock tower collapsing into the flames drew widespread shock and anger, and GuÃ©rin, who was in tears when he first saw the scale of the damage this week, believes the reaction is "legitimate and completely understandable".

Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protests

Limoges city hall was set on fire last weekend with its wooden clock tower collapsing on Saturday

What is apparent from the array of flowers and sombre onlookers gathered at the hall's entrance, is that this is a town mourning the loss, or at the least the harm inflicted on its most iconic and, frankly, most beautiful building.

GuÃ©rin blames the damage on the French hard left, "supported by rioters". Two men have been arrested, a 66-year-old, as well as another suspect who is 34. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks".

Limoges' conservative mayor claims he has received a message of support from US Vice President JD Vance, but not Emmanual Macron, his own, outgoing president.

"What happened here will have an influence on the upcoming presidential election. This country is not doing well at all," he says.

Two men have been arrested in connection with the fire. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks"

For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.

In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.

In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.

Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.

Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.

Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask.

Jade, a 19-year-old medical student, says she has to get by on â¬300 per month and is frustrated by French politics

"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.

It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.

I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with â¬500,000 (Â£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?

"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.

Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."

She complains of having to live on â¬300 per month.

"I feel we are not respected as young adults."

Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.

This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.

In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century.

"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."

Jean Roger Faucher got married in Limoges town hall. He says he cannot accept protests when they put people's lives at risk

Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that.

"On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.

Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease.

"Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.

Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.

Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.

In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.

With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.

#200. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on October 24, 2026

The Moon is only a few nights away from reaching its full phase. If you're planning to take a look tonight, here's what to know about its current appearance and what you might spot on its surface.

As of Saturday, Oct. 24, NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 95% of its surface visible.

Tonight, without the use of visual aids you should be able to spot the Mares Imbrium, Serenitatis, Fecunditatis. If you have binoculars you'll also see the Endymion Crater, the Alphonsus Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. Finally, if you have a telescope, you'll also see the Apollo 16 and 17 landing spots, and the Schiller Crater.

The next Full Moon will take place on October 25 or 26, depending on your timezone.

The Moon takes around 29.5 days to travel around Earth, and its appearance changes throughout the month. As it moves around our planet, we see different amounts of its sunlit side, from a slim crescent to the quarter phases and eventually a Full Moon. It then begins the cycle again. As NASA explains, these phases are caused by the Moon's changing position relative to Earth and the Sun.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Lois also holds a Master's degree in Digital Journalism from Strathclyde University and obtained a Master of Arts in English Literature at the University of Aberdeen.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said the conflicts threatening free shipping, such as the Iran-backed Houthi rebels firing at vessels in the Red Sea, could not be solved militarily.

Wadephul is attending a summit in Istanbul, joined by foreign ministers from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Egypt, France and the UK.

Commenting on the ongoing crises in the Red Sea and off the coast of Ukraine, the German minister said his country was willing to negotiate with Iran, together with France and the UK.

The three European countries were among the signatories of the 2015 JCPOA deal with Iran which was torn up by Donald Trump during his first term in office.

Wadephul also urged Russia to make a deal to secure shipping in the Black Sea.

Vincent Kompany, the coach of the Bundesliga's Bayern Munich, was hospitalized on Friday, according to team officials.

"​Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during a ​training session for Bayern’s reserve team," ​the ‌club said. "The head coach of the professional squad had been observing the second team's session."

"Kompany is ‌currently undergoing a thorough examination in the ‌hospital ​and will remain under medical care. For the time being, his coaching staff will manage all training and match-related ​operations."

Currently leading the Bundesliga, Bayern drew 2-2 in a Champions League match against UK's Arsenal this week.

“Vincent Kompany’s health is our top priority," ​said Max Eberl, ‌Bayern's Board Member for Sport.

"Vinnie is receiving all the necessary ⁠medical care ​and support, and he will be given as much time as he needs. Everyone at FC Bayern wishes Vinnie a quick recovery."

After hackers targeted Germany's far-right AfD party and published hundreds of thousands of internal emails online this week, German magazine Der Spiegel published a report highlighting a 2017 exchange regarding illegal donations from Switzerland.

German parties are legally forbidden from receiving donations from non-EU countries.

The scandal already prompted a formal probe in 2018, which ended with authorities imposing fines that amounted to over half a million euros (around $565,000). German prosecutors also opened a formal probe into the party's prominent co-leader, Alice Weidel. The probe was closed in 2021 due to insufficient evidence.

Weidel has claimed that she only learned of the "unsolicited" donations in September 2017 and decided to return the money due to "legal concerns."

But the recently leaked emails indicate Weidel told a regional party treasurer to be on the lookout for "possible incoming donations" in July 2017, just days before the money started coming in. In August, the treasurer referred to a "benefactor from Switzerland" who supports Weidel with thousands of Swiss francs per week.

When contacted by the AFP news agency on Friday, Weidel's spokesperson said the AfD leader was not revising "any of her statements regarding the matter."

"Ms. Weidel neither expected specific amounts nor was she certain that individual persons would actually donate" and did not expect the payments from Switzerland, her press representative said.

Germany’s far-right AfD is investigating the extent of the damage from a massive data breach. Hackers copied hundreds of thousands of emails and sensitive documents.

The data has been published online, and the first excerpts are slowly being made public. The AfD has reported the matter to the relevant authorities and appealed to the media not to publish "stolen" data.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will travel to Japan, Singapore and South Korea next week for meetings on economic and security policy, according to deputy government spokesman Steffen Meyer.

"We share with ‌all three countries ‌a ​commitment to open, rules-based trade and a ​desire to strengthen economic ⁠resilience and ​security, ​particularly with regard ​to global ‌supply chains," said Meyer during a Friday press conference.

Merz is scheduled to depart Berlin on Monday and return Friday. He will be accompanied by a German business delegation.

All three countries possess "great innovative power," said Meyer, "that is why we want to deepen collaboration on future-relevant topics such a AI."

Merz will begin his trip by visiting Singapore on Tuesday, where he will meet the prime minister and president before delivering a speech.

On Wednesday, he will travel to Tokyo to meet the prime minister and take part in a German-Japanese economic summit.

Merz will end his trip in South Korea where he will meet with the president before kicking off the 19th annual Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business (APK), in Seoul.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned that continuing disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea could potentially lead to famine in the global south.

"We're all feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping lanes, whether at the gas station or in the supermarket," he said ahead of a meeting with fellow foreign ministers in Istanbul on Friday. "But elsewhere, there is a threat of famine when fertilizers don't arrive in the places where they are essential for basic production."

Wadephul was referring not only to the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi threats to the Bab al-Mandab strait, but also to Russian attacks on shipping in the Black Sea as part of Moscow's ongoing war against Ukraine, one of the world's leading producers of wheat.

"This effects the poorest people in the world whose basic provisions are especially dependent on wheat, as well as our partners such as Turkey, the biggest wheat processing country in the world," he said.

"Together, we want to send a signal: we will not accept Iran and the Houthi militias [in Yemen] holding global trade hostage," Wadephul continued.

"The indiscriminatory attacks on free shipping and on neighboring countries must stop. For people across the region who are suffering from hunger, who no longer feel safe in their own homes, the continuing insecurity is not acceptable."

German Federal Prosecutors said Friday that a judge from the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe had ordered the detention of a Ukrainian man arrested by police in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Thursday.

The man is accused of spying on German and NATO military installations in the country on behalf of Russian intelligence services.

Investigators say he sought to collect information on the production of armored vehicles, explosives and munitions. Moreover, he collected information on military personnel and facilities tasked with protecting NATO's eastern flank.

The President of Pakistan, Asif Ali Zardari, was expected to be received with military honors in Berlin on Friday, at the start of a two-day visit to mark the 75th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Pakistan and Germany.

The Pakistani foreign ministry said in a statement that Zardari will hold meetings with his German counterpart, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, as well as with senior business leaders.

The statement placed a particular focus on "economic and trade cooperation" and said the visit "reflects the deep commitment of both countries to the further strengthening the partnership."

Like President Steinmeier in Germany, President Zardari is Pakistan's official head of state, a largely ceremonial role. Real political power in Pakistan lies theoretically with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and currently de facto with the influential head of the armed forces, Field Marshall Asim Munir.

Partly for that reason, Berlin's Tagesspiegel newspaper expressed skepticism over Zardari's visit, describing him as a "powerless president," highlighting past corruption scandals, criticizing the treatment of German media outlets in Pakistan and questioning why Germany was investing political capital in deeper relations with the Islamic Republic.

The newspaper opined that Islamabad's mediatory role in the Middle East isn't as influential as it seems and suggested that Pakistan's neighbor and rival India was a significantly more important trading partner for both Germany and the European Union.

It did say acknowledge that "Germany cannot ignore Pakistan" as a nuclear power on the frontline of climate change and as a country with a rapidly growing population, but ultimately concluded that Zardari's visit was more "FOMO" (fear of missing out) than real diplomatic "strategy."

The Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), begins its two-day party conference in Munich on Friday.

Together, the CDU and CSU form Germany's center-right "Union" and, despite plunging ratings for Merz and the CDU nationally, backing for the CSU in Bavaria remains relatively strong, with two recent polls putting support at between 36% and 37%.

Nevertheless, there is still concern in Munich that the Union's struggles in the coalition government in Berlin and growing support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), including in Bavaria, could threaten the CSU's status as a "big tent party" or Volkspartei.

Chancellor Merz will address delegates on Saturday but few in Munich are hopeful of a positive change of course. And all the while, CSU leader and Bavarian State Premier Markus Söder remains waiting in the wings as a potential challenger to Merz at the national level.

The charismatic, self-confident 59-year-old dominates Bavarian politics and, according to sources who spoke to the DPA news agency, would be ready to step up if called upon.

But a leadership challenge is not expected to be a serious proposition until April 2027 when another senior Union figure and potential chancellor candidate, Hendrik Wüst (CDU), runs in local elections in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), where he is currently serving as state premier.

For this weekend, however, the conservatives' focus is on Bavaria.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (CDU) was expected in Istanbul, Turkey, on Friday ahead of a meeting with his Turkish, Saudi Arabian, Pakistani, Egyptian, French and British counterparts.

The foreign ministers are set to discuss a range of geopolitical issues including, according to a spokesperson for the Turkish foreign ministry, "the Palestine question, the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, developments in Yemen and the search for an end to the war in Ukraine."

For the seven ministers, the event marks a first such meeting in the so-called "R4+E3" format. The E3, consisting of Germany, France and the United Kingdom, was established in the early 2000s amid nuclear negotiations with Iran, while Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt formed the R4 earlier this year to coordinate a joint regional response to the US-Israeli war on Iran.

"At our first meeting in this format, we Europeans and the four regional powers want to discuss together how we can inject fresh impetus into the conflicts in the Strait of Hormuz, around [the] Bab al-Mandab [strait] and in the Black Sea," said Wadephul ahead of his departure.

"We can only deal with these massive challenges if we work together beyond established formats," he continued, adding that "these gridlocked conflicts" which have "significant economic and security consequences for our countries" have also created a fresh "desire to look for new solutions."

#203. US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran

Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis

Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.

The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.

The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”

Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.

Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.

The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.

The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.

The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.

Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”

He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.

“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”

Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.

“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

#205. Are California voters about to impose world's first 'tax on billionaires'?

Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions and being home to many rich and famous.

Now voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them - names that include media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.

Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.

There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".

But the vote is also offering regular everyday residents a voice on an issue that has riled politics for decades.

"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.

The state has the largest economy in the country - and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the whole of the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the globe. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.

Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (Â£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.

Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.

"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she told the BBC.

While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.

The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.

California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.

While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries â Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.

Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue, she said.

In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax

The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.

They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.

Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax.

"I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he added, saying the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.

DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".

Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax

Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said, external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believes the way the measure is written is "problematic", it is necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.

Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy.

"I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief executive said in an interview with the BBC's news partner in the US, CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."

Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.

While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th century, that they have a God-given right to rule".

"They have all the wealth; they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on Nov 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson".

Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels, external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.

Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey, external from the Public Policy Institute of California.

Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment that is behind a policy" like Prop 40.

"This is really not about Prop 40," he says. It's about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".

US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.
