#557. France: Protesters clash with police in nationwide protests, amid rising social polarization

Unrest broke out in parts of France as students, trade unionists and Yellow Vest activists took to the streets to protest high prices and inequality. Police arrested over 1,000 people amid chaotic scenes.

Police and protesters clashed amid mass rallies across France on Saturday, over high prices and social inequalities and the state of the education system.

France's Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said some 1,200 people had been arrested across the country and that 150 police officers had been injured.

"It's a miracle the toll wasn't higher," Lecornu said while visiting officers deployed in Paris on Saturday evening.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 110,000 people took part in the demonstrations in Paris alone, while 110 marches had taken place across the country.

The Interior Ministry said some 550,000 people turned out for the nationwide demonstrations.

The ministry said the arrests were made following violent incidents in Paris, Marseilles, Rennes, Toulouse, Angers and other cities across the country.

"Such actions include attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets," the ministry said, blaming the unrest on what it described ​as the "hard-left."

In Paris and Marseille, police fired tear gas at protesters as violent clashes took place.

AFP reported that dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Bordeaux and Lille.

The windows of the offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in western Paris were also broken by protesters, and AFP journalists reported seeing several parked cars torched.

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence in a post on X and warned: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."

In Lyon, situated in central France, the city's tourism office was set alight with flames and black smoke seen billowing from the building.

In the city of Limoges, the town hall was set alight as unrest broke out. The blaze spread from a wing of the building and eventually reached the roof, where it continued burning as crowds stood watching.

The historic building was largely destroyed by the blaze, despite attempts by firefighters to douse the flames.

Meanwhile, in the northern city of Lille, protesters smashed their way into the city hall and vandalized the premises before leaving, according to an AFP photographer.

Riot police within minutes confirmed that all the protesters had left.

The protests come on the heels of an initial wave of demonstrations that began last month over the situation at schools in the country, with pupils complaining about teacher absences and run-down facilities.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the French capital, police had banned rallies around the Elysee presidential palace, the prime minister's office and the Champs-Elysees avenue, along with other key locations.

A march through the center of the city was also banned.

Reports began emerging late on Saturday morning of riot police clashing with protesters in the Saint-Denis area on the outskirts of the capital, as well as near the Gare du Nord train station, among other areas.

In Paris, DW correspondent Jack Parrock said unrest was playing out in small pockets of the city.

"The videos circulating on social media of the violence in France don’t paint the full picture," Parrock said.

"The significant percentage of the people we met out on the streets of Paris were teachers, nurses, students, and workers, who want no part in the unrest, but do also seem to understand why the outbreaks are happening," Parrock explained.

"Amongst those people, we did still witness a collective rage against a government they don’t feel is listening to them," said Parrock.

On the matter of how police were responding, Parrock said they had seen police "seemingly try to show some restraint — clearly intending to de-escalate some of the recent tension."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Students have been joined by trade unionists and remnants of the Yellow Vests ("Gilets jaunes") movement, which staged mass weekly protests from November 2018 to June 2020, initially against rising fuel prices. They later morphed into protests against the high cost of living and economic inequality in general.

The student protests over the past weeks have been backed by Jean-Luc Melenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed ("La France insoumise", or LFI), who marched in one demonstration on Tuesday.

The government has blamed the LFI for pouring fuel on the fire of widespread public discontent, an allegation the party has denied.

Edited by: Karl Sexton, Jenipher Camino, Sean Sinico

#558. Apples Pro and Tell MacBook event is almost here: Everything we expect

Apple isn't done with new product releases quite yet.

Fall has proven to be quite a busy season for Apple, with the September iPhone event, which saw the grand debut of the new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Apple then followed up with the "Welcome Home" smart home launch event earlier this month, where the company unveiled its new HomeView device alongside a slew of other products.

Apple is now preparing for an Oct. 28 event in Los Angeles. What does Apple have in store next? The invitations for the event went out with the tagline "Pro and Tell," so all signs point to a new MacBook Pro. In fact, we fully expect that Apple will reveal the long-awaited touchscreen OLED MacBook.

However, we all know Apple loves a "One More Thing" approach, and we're following rumors on a few new devices. Here's everything we expect to learn at the "Pro and Tell" special event next week.

Apple has never released a MacBook with a touchscreen or OLED display, so this is a big deal.

Bloomberg's Apple insider Mark Gurman says the touchscreen MacBook will have a different design than the current MacBook Pro models. The laptop will be thinner and lighter, and the OLED display will allow for thinner bezels on the device. Apple is also expected to replace the notch with a hole-punch camera with a Dynamic Island, much like the iPhone, according to Gurman.

Don't get too excited, though, unless you're ready to pay a premium for Apple's upcoming new laptop. The touchscreen OLED MacBook won't be cheap.

The existing MacBook Pro lineup starts at $1,999 for the 14-inch M5 chip model and $2,499 for the 16-inch M5 Pro chipset model. So, a touchscreen OLED model could get pricey.

While Apple may not be launching touchscreen MacBooks with the M6 chip, the company is expected to launch refreshed versions of its current MacBook Pro with the new chipset.

Apple unveiled its first M6 device with the new Mac mini in August. The company seems on track to roll out the M6 chip to the MacBook Pro and iMac next.

Based on how Apple rolled out the M5 chip last year, and Gurman's latest reports, don't be surprised to see a new entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro launched on Oct. 28 with the M6 chip.

There's also a rumor of an updated iMac launching at the event as well. The iMac hasn't seen a refresh since 2024, when the M4 model was released. If a new M6 iMac is indeed unveiled, there could be new color options as well.

The last iPad mini was launched in 2024 with the A17 Pro chip, which was the chipset powering the iPhone 15 Pro. It's well time for a refresh, and it seems like we will be getting one.

Apple has been rumored to be working on its first water-resistant iPad, and it appears that the new iPad mini will be that device, although it's unclear as to what level it will be water-resistant.

The new iPad mini is expected to be powered by the new A20 Pro chip, have an OLED display with thinner bezels, and a new front-facing selfie camera, according to MacRumors.

We're speculating here a bit, but Apple is reportedly taking a creator-centric approach to its Oct. 28 special event. In addition, 9to5Mac reported this week that Apple keeps acquiring companies with a specific strategy in mind: Improving its Apple Creator Studio subscription offering.

If Apple did want to announce updates to Creator Studio, then a creator-focused event like this would be the perfect opportunity.

Will Apple also unveil any unexpected surprises? We'll have to wait and see on Oct. 28.

#559. ‘The Cycle’ Is a Surprising New Take on the Police Procedural, With a Huge Twist and an Emotional Resonance the Director Didn’t Expect

SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “The Cycle,” now streaming on Shudder.

What if a werewolf continued to transform even after its death?

This light bulb idea came to frequent collaborators Jordan Downey and Kevin Stewart as they were sketching out a TV treatment for their 2018 film “The Head Hunter.” Related Stories Bestseller 'The Story of Marceau Miller' Adaptation Set for Mipcom via France TV Distribution (EXCLUSIVE)

“We both looked at each other and stopped and were like, ‘Wait, that’s a really cool, fun idea and a take on werewolves that we’ve never seen before,’” Downey says. “Being the horror cinephiles that we are, we were like, ‘I don’t think anyone’s done that. I can’t think of a movie or a show.’ We Googled it and realized, no, it hasn’t been done. What do you do with that idea?” Popular on Variety

The result is “The Cycle,” a handsomely shot detective story following Meg (Deborah Ann Woll) and Marks (Jeffrey Donovan) as experts trying to solve a lycanthropic murder mystery — although the film largely keeps the exact supernatural entity a mystery, until the third act goes full creature feature.

Downey, who co-wrote the film with Stewart and directed it, thought that outsized hook would benefit from a recognizable framing.

“Right away, it felt like it fit best into a crime mystery, a police procedural,” he says. “Ultimately, if you have this werewolf that is going to reanimate and then at dawn turn back into a man — but in this case it’s a deceased man who doesn’t move, walk, talk, has no life — that would just be dumbfounding to police. They would come into this crime scene and they would see these victims, but then they’d find this naked dead guy not knowing that he’s harboring something supernatural. So it made sense that there really wasn’t another package to put it into.”

Once the case is cracked, the third act shifts hard into monster movie mode, complete with plenty of practical blood, guts and werewolf nastiness.

“I love creature features,” Downey says. “I didn’t want it to be this ‘elevated,’ pretentious experience that didn’t give monster movie fans the proper experience. You go into ‘The Cycle’ not knowing that’s what’s coming. I thought what would happen is the characters would be thrust into a completely crazy change in their lives, that they now exist in a world where werewolves can be real and there’s one in proximity to them. That change would be as shocking to them as it hopefully would be to the audience. So we were aware of trying to do things early in the movie, so when that tonal shift happens, it felt earned but also surprising.”

Ushering in the change of pace was the transformation scene, which is one of the most loved traditions in werewolf movies and was exciting for the team to plan for, along with key special effects artist and supervisor Patrick Magee.

“The first thing was acknowledging that if you’re going to make a werewolf movie, we didn’t want to run from that challenge,” Downey says. “In the ’80s, Rob Bottin and Rick Baker nailed it with ‘The Howling’ and ‘An American Werewolf in London.’ In the years since, people have shied away from it because either it’s too expensive, too time-consuming or maybe there’s a clever new way of doing it. But we just felt like enough time had gone where we hadn’t seen that done very well for so many years. So we said right away, ‘If we’re going to do this, we have to do a proper werewolf transformation. We have to nail it.’ We storyboarded it a lot. We talked about it a lot. We broke down the best scenes that had been done and thought about … Do we want to see foot? Do we want to see hands? Do we want to see eyes, teeth? Is it a spinal cord? All of the different things that we wanted to see in our scene, and then how it would apply to an undead corpse version of a transformation.

Beyond the horror element, the film examines the complex choices that can come with fatherhood, which comes most notably via Meg, who learns that her long-lost parent is the werewolf at the heart of the story.

“It wasn’t in the first drafts, to be honest,” Downey says. “In our initial treatments, Meg was investigating a stranger. It was the same concept that a man’s body was discovered, the police didn’t know how he was tied to these murders, and they went to her because she was an expert in her field, but he wasn’t her father. We got her into Act Three, when she went to the house, just like in the movie where they go to investigate his whereabouts and the life of the recluse. We felt like she was putting herself in this really dangerous position, without some kind of an emotional tie to that character. I told Kevin that I don’t believe that the character would do this given the circumstances. We were also missing something that I thought is really important in horror films, which is the heart and the pathos of a monster movie and the tragedy. So then, we came up with the idea that, ‘OK, what if this is her father?’ So now we’ve anchored something to her emotionally. We can work in the tragedy of this man who left, but it was in her mind for a terrible reason, a father walking out on their children. In his mind, it was to protect them. And once we had that for her father, then we started to apply that theme to some of the other characters.”

Much like the cycle of undead werewolves, it’s easy to see this story carry on through new chapters. Downey says he’s happy keeping “The Cycle” as a single story, but has also mulled over what a larger scope could be.

“I think this movie is self-contained and there’s versions of it that I would probably not be interested in,” Downey says. “But we did talk a lot about different stories. I think there’s a great prequel in the original werewolf that came from over the sea. There’s an aquatic, boat-set version of this story that I think would be interesting. You could do a TV series about the life and the trials of [Meg’s father] Peter Stump and all of the different things that he was doing while isolated for those 30 years. I think it’d be interesting to see … because she’s so good at her job, and in the final scene of the movie so confident that she’s gonna get this figured out. But what if she didn’t? What if 10, 15, 20 years goes by and she has not solved it and she is now facing the same dilemma her dad was, which was, ‘This fucking thing can’t be stopped.’ But by killing herself, that does nothing. Finding her at a point of quit would be really interesting. I’d only want to do stuff if Deborah and Jeffrey wanted to come back and work on it again, and if there were fans that wanted it to happen, but I would never say no.”

#560. Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Severe sunburn increases the risk of developing melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer.Credit: Olga Pankova/Getty

A personalized mRNA vaccine reduced the risk of skin cancer returning or the recipient dying by 42% when used alongside an immunotherapy drug, according to long-awaited results for what could become the first approved mRNA vaccine for cancer.

Oncologists regard a risk reduction of 10% as substantial, says Kristen Radford, an immunotherapist at Mater Research in Brisbane. A risk reduction of more than 40% “would send many researchers over the Moon”, adds Seth Cheetham, a geneticist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.

The personalized vaccine, called intismeran, is not designed to prevent skin cancer, or melanoma, from developing in the first place, but to stop it returning in people who have already undergone surgery to remove tumours.

Anticipation for the trial results has been building since August, when the vaccine’s developers — Merck, based in Rahway, New Jersey, and Moderna, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts — announced early positive results. Data from the phase III trial will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid on 24 October. But when data were leaked online on 22 October, the companies released the key results.

The stock price for Moderna, a pioneer in mRNA vaccine technology, had been rising since the August announcement, but dropped by around 25% after the leak. Health-care financial analyst Evan Seigerman at BMO Capital Markets in New York City told media company Forbes that such reactions in the stock market probably reflect “inflated expectation into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy”.

The intismeran trial enrolled 1,137 people with moderate to advanced melanoma across 157 centres. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a tailor-made vaccine (intismeran) alongside the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab — which is already used to treat melanoma — or pembrolizumab plus an inactive placebo. Trial leader Georgina Long, an oncologist at Melanoma Institute Australia in Sydney, says participants have so far been followed for around 25 months and will continue to be monitored for several years to determine whether the vaccine improves overall survival. She adds that the therapy did not result in any major harmful side effects.

Roughly 15 years ago, people with advanced melanoma typically survived for only months. Today, nearly 55% are effectively cured with targeted drugs or immunotherapies, says Long. The combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab is designed for people whose cancer could return after surgery and who do not respond to immunotherapy alone, she says.

Jessamy Tiffen, a cancer geneticist at the Centenary Institute in Sydney, says that the trial results are exciting, but that only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years. “Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them,” she says. Furthermore, some people did not respond to the vaccine, she says.

Long says that her team will conduct a statistical analysis to identify who is most likely to benefit from the treatment.

To develop intismeran, Long and her colleagues sequenced DNA from a sample of each participant’s tumour to identify mutations in the cancer cells. These mutations can give rise to proteins called neoantigens, which help to distinguish cancer cells from healthy ones.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03417-0

#561. The Best Art TV Deals: Samsung Frame, Hisense Canvas, and More (2026)

We're big fans of art TVs here at WIRED. They're perfect for people who don't want a TV to be the constant center of attention in their living room. No art TV maker is better than the pioneer: Samsung. Specifically, Samsung's The Frame Pro series of TVs. The 2026 models (LS03HW) add tons of new features, including more intuitive software, a higher refresh rate for gaming, and even better picture quality.

The problem with The Frame Pro has always been the price. The smallest 55-inch model dropped to $1,098 during Prime Day earlier this month, and I've been happy to see that the price has stayed around. (In fact, earlier this week, it dropped by an additional $100 to its lowest price ever.) Seeing it discounted to under $1,000 was fantastic, but even at $1,098, it's a really solid deal. It was selling for $200 more in September and for the full retail price of $1,498 in August. Beyond the smallest 55-inch model, you also have size options for The Frame Pro of a 65-inch, 75-inch, or 85-inch TV.

Samsung also has an entry-level version of The Frame, which has an even deeper discount right now. It's just $898, which is $100 off its Prime Day price—the cheapest it's even been! It's actually the same price as the older 2025 model.

We haven't tested this model yet ourselves, but the main difference between The Frame and The Frame Pro is the brightness and image quality. They both use a matte finish, but The Frame Pro has nearly double the max brightness, while the standard Frame only goes up to around 650 nits. The Frame Pro also comes with a wireless connect box for a cleaner and simpler setup. It's definitely the one to get if you can swing the extra $200.

As we have documented, there's been an explosion of interest in art TVs in 2026, with competitors like Amazon, Hisense, and TCL joining the game. We've tested many of these new options—many of which try to undercut The Frame in price. The one on sale right now that I'd point to is the Hisense S7 CanvasTV (55S7SG). It's not even as bright as the standard Frame, but at $750 (for the 55-inch size), it's the cheapest art TV you can buy right now.

With Black Friday coming up next month, it's certainly possible that prices on these art TVs will drop even more. The 2025 Samsung Frame and Frame Pro both dropped to their lowest prices during Black Friday last year. It's a gamble—you could wait for Black Friday or get a sure thing right now.

#562. Billboard Latin Music Week 2026 Photo Booth: Anuel AA, Becky G, Maluma & More

See some of the photo booth gems captured backstage throughout the week.

Billboard Latin Music Week 2026 brought some of the biggest Latin music stars to Miami for a weeklong conference, including Anuel AA, Becky G, Fuerza Regida, Kany García, Lali, Maluma, Mau & Ricky, and many more. The artists – who spoke at panels and/or performed at showcases – also posed for Billboard’s photo booth.

Among the artists sitting for Icon or Superstar Q&As were Puerto Rican singer-songwriter Kany García, música mexicana powerhouse Fuerza Regida, Colombian superstar Maluma, Mexican-American singer and actress Becky G, Panamanian legend Rubén Blades and Cuban-American global megastar Pitbull.

Meanwhile, Venezuelan trippy-pop band Rawayana shared the story behind their touring success in a panel presented by Live Nation, along with Latin Power Players Executive of the Year Hans Schafer; married couples Jessi Uribe and Paola Jara, and Jay Wheeler and Zhamira, joined together on stage for a conversation about Love & Music; and Ana Mena, Aria Vega, Greeicy, LALI, Lola Indigo and RaiNao were the stars of the Women’s Panel: Global Rising.

This year’s Billboard En Vivo showcases where in charge of Fuerza Regida (Oct. 20) and Jay Wheeler and Zhamira (Oct. 21). Speakers also included Bebeshito, Carlos Rivera, Clave Especial, Grupo Frontera, Grupo Niche, Quevedo, Ryan Castro and more.

Latin Music Week also coincided with the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards, which aired Thursday, Oct. 22, on Telemundo and Peacock. During the ceremony, Cristian Castro, Fuerza Regida, Rosalía and Rubén Blades received special awards, while Fuerza Regida was the biggest winner with eight trophies.

#563. People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

An experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting users willing to obtain unapproved versions online. Now, scientists are using artificial intelligence to investigate their experiences, uncovering unexpected symptom reports that differ from those documented in clinical trials.

The drug, retatrutide, belongs to a new generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight. Although it remains under investigation and is not approved for use, people are purchasing unapproved formulations that are not intended for human consumption and discussing their experiences on internet forums.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 users to investigate these accounts. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open, provides the first systematic examination of potential side effects reported by people claiming to use unapproved retatrutide.

One finding stood out. Among users whose reported symptoms could be classified, increased appetite was the most common complaint. That was particularly unexpected because retatrutide is designed to suppress hunger, and its Phase 2 clinical trials primarily identified digestive problems as the most frequent side effects.

AI Uncovers Unexpected Weight-Loss Drug Reports

"Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people's self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Director of Penn's Computational Social Listening Lab and senior author of the study.

However, the researchers emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as proof of previously unknown side effects. Reddit users represent a very different population from clinical trial participants, and their accounts cannot establish whether the drug caused the symptoms they described.

There is also considerable uncertainty about what these individuals are actually taking. Products sold outside regulated medical channels may differ from the genuine experimental medication in their ingredients, purity, and dosage.

"We can't say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit users are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary," says Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author of the study.

Rather than confirming new risks, the research offers scientists an opportunity to identify questions that warrant more rigorous investigation.

"This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials," says Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS.

How Researchers Analyzed 150,000 Reddit Posts

The project builds on previous research by the University of Pennsylvania team. In that earlier investigation, scientists used large language models (LLMs), the type of artificial intelligence that powers many modern chatbots, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts discussing semaglutide and tirzepatide.

That analysis revealed reports of possible side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully documented in clinical trials or official drug safety records.

"We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide," says Sehgal.

Retatrutide is particularly interesting because it works differently from existing GLP-1 medications. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor involved in blood sugar control and appetite regulation, while tirzepatide targets two. Retatrutide activates three receptors, potentially producing a different combination of effects throughout the body.

To investigate what people were experiencing, the researchers used AI to examine nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments. They identified approximately 14,000 users who claimed to have personally taken an unapproved version of retatrutide.

The AI systems then extracted descriptions of symptoms that users associated with the medication and translated those descriptions into standardized medical terminology. This allowed researchers to compare reports even when different people used different words to describe similar experiences.

After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and reduced appetite, the team identified 7,823 users who reported at least one symptom that could be medically classified.

"A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking," says Sehgal. "AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize."

The most striking difference involved hunger.

In retatrutide's Phase 2 clinical trials (the drug is currently in Phase 3 trials, the final step before FDA approval), participants most commonly experienced gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea. These effects are familiar concerns with medications that influence appetite and digestion.

But among Reddit users who reported taking unapproved retatrutide, the pattern looked different. Increased appetite emerged as the most frequently described classifiable symptom, despite the substantial weight-loss effects demonstrated in clinical testing.

The researchers also compared the new findings with their earlier analysis of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Compared with those earlier Reddit reports, discussions involving unapproved retatrutide contained proportionally more mentions of appetite-related changes, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. Reports of nausea and other digestive complaints were proportionally less common.

These differences could reflect how retatrutide interacts with the body. However, they could also result from differences between the groups of people discussing the medications, their other drug use, or the contents of the unapproved products.

"Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it's possible that its effects on the body are different, too," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study.

"But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different," she notes. "Users willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can't verify exactly what they're taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean."

Can AI Detect Drug Safety Concerns Earlier?

Beyond the findings about retatrutide, the study demonstrates how AI could potentially improve the early detection of drug safety concerns.

Traditional monitoring systems depend heavily on clinical trials, reports submitted to regulators, and information collected by healthcare professionals. People obtaining experimental medications through unapproved channels may not be represented in those systems.

Social media offers another source of information, allowing researchers to identify recurring experiences that might otherwise escape attention. However, these reports must be independently investigated before they can be considered reliable evidence of a drug-related problem.

The Penn team has already seen an example of how this approach can help guide further research.

In their previous investigation of semaglutide and tirzepatide, researchers identified online reports of menstrual irregularities. Those findings subsequently encouraged another scientific team to examine similar symptoms using the FDA's database of reported adverse drug events.

The follow-up study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, also detected disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes. Although those findings did not establish causation, they provided additional reasons to investigate the potential connection.

The researchers hope their retatrutide findings will lead to similar independent studies, particularly as the drug advances through clinical development.

"That's what we hope will happen with this study," says Sehgal. "Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing."

The research was conducted through the University of Pennsylvania's School of Engineering and Applied Science and Perelman School of Medicine. Benjamin Rader of Boston Children's Hospital also contributed as a co-author. Funding was provided in part by the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. Tronieri disclosed receiving an investigator-initiated grant from Novo Nordisk on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, along with consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. No conflicts of interest were reported by the other authors.

#564. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

#565. ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3 Explained: Does Joanne Finally Convert to Judaism? What Happens to Morgan and Sasha?

Here's a breakdown of the Netflix rom-com's biggest moments in its third season. Spoilers ahead...

[This story contains MAJOR spoilers from Nobody Wants This season three.]

Like clockwork, fall means another new season of Nobody Wants This — and after three seasons, we finally have an answer to what happens with Noah and Joanne’s interfaith relationship.

The Netflix rom-com has returned with all 10 episodes of its third season currently streaming, picking up with the couple more serious than ever. They’ve moved in together, and Joanne is attending Jewish conversion classes as she and Noah look to build a future together. Related Stories Business Apple's Newest iPhone May Be Hollywood's Best Friend Movies Jeon Do-yeon Defined an Era of Korean Cinema. With 'Possible Love,' She's Become an Oscar Contender

Below, The Hollywood Reporter breaks down the season’s biggest moments, from surprise cameos and new relationships to romantic twists that threaten to complicate things. Read on to find out what happens in season three of Nobody Wants This.

In episode four, Noah (Adam Brody) and Joanne (Kristen Bell) take the next step in their relationship by attending their first wedding together. Noah tells Joanne he has to officiate his friend Brian’s wedding, so she accompanies him as his plus one. However, they nearly miss their flight when Joanne offers her seat to a superfan, Nicole (played in a cameo by series creator Erin Foster). They meet at the airport because the woman reminds her of herself.

Ultimately, they make their flight and head to wine country, where Noah reveals that Brian isn’t real and the wedding was a ploy to get Joanne there so he could propose. With Taylor Swift’s “Lover” playing in the background, the two are officially engaged!

Foster told Netflix Tudum that she was inspired by her own 2019 engagement to her now-husband, Simon Tikhman. “I thought I was going to [another couple’s] vow renewal, and I wasn’t. I was going to my own proposal,” she said. “All roads lead back to me every time.”

The moment some viewers have been waiting for all season finally happens in episode seven: Morgan (Justine Lupe) and Sasha (Timothy Simons) cross the line from friends to lovers. Their relationship reaches a turning point when, at Morgan’s request, Sasha joins her on a trip to New York City, where she appears on Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen for her new podcast segment, “Make Them.”

The pair go to dinner, which Sasha calls a date — and Morgan doesn’t correct him — before taking a walk, where Morgan opens up to him more than ever before about her former marriage. They nearly share their first kiss, but Morgan pulls back, insisting that once they cross that boundary, there’s no going back. After all, their siblings are now engaged.

But when they return to the hotel, a few more attempts to resist their chemistry prove futile and they finally give in. However, the morning after changes everything (more on that below).

Following her separation from Sasha, Esther (Jackie Tohn) begins exploring life outside her marriage. Although she initially tells him that dating isn’t her priority, that changes as the season progresses. When Morgan tries to help Sasha move on by creating an online dating profile for him, he discovers Esther is on the app, too, making it clear that she’s putting herself out there and that he should do the same.

Esther also pursues a career in real estate, earning her license and meeting Julian (Steven Weber), a wealthy, older client. The two hit it off and eventually decide to date exclusively.

After their romantic night in New York City, Morgan walks out on Sasha the next morning, leaving a note saying she caught an earlier flight. After some time to process her feelings, she realizes she made a mistake and tells Sasha she wants to give their relationship another chance. However, he rejects her, explaining that he isn’t emotionally ready to risk their friendship.

The rejection leaves Morgan unable to stand being in the same room as Sasha, making Noah and Joanne’s wedding planning even more complicated. But that’s not the only relationship drama brewing. In the finale, Esther visits Sasha at his home to drop something off for their daughter and the estranged couple ends up hooking up. The encounter threatens Esther’s relationship with Julian and adds another layer to the already messy Morgan-Sasha dynamic.

The Bravo love is strong in season three. Early on, Noah mentions Summer House when he interrupts Joanne while she’s bed-rotting and tells her to stop bingeing the beloved reality series so they can talk.

A few episodes later, Morgan appears on Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen for her new podcast segment, with Cohen himself making a cameo in a taped segment of his talk show. Her fellow guest is none other than Ciara Miller, who has starred on Summer House since season five. Miller has also made headlines this year amid the drama surrounding her best friend and castmate Amanda Batula’s relationship with West Wilson, Miller’s ex and another Summer House star.

With the penultimate episode of the season centered on Christmas, it seemed like the perfect opportunity to celebrate Chrismukkah — the hybrid Christmas-and-Hanukkah holiday popularized by Seth Cohen (also played by Brody) on Fox’s hit early-2000s series The O.C.

Instead, the episode focuses on Noah trying to make sure Joanne has the best Christmas possible. With her conversion to Judaism approaching, he wants to make the holiday special for her as she prepares for a new chapter in her life. The Christmas episode offers a sweet moment for the couple before the season’s emotional finale.

One of the biggest questions hanging over the series since season one is finally answered: Will Joanne convert to Judaism? Throughout the season, Joanne takes conversion classes taught by Rabbi Eden (Sarah Silverman), alongside Sebastien (Andrew Rannells). In the finale, she reaches the final step: the mikvah, a ritual immersion that marks her conversion.

The emotional moment takes place in the ocean near the Malibu Beach house where the two families have gathered. As Joanne enters the water and emerges following the ritual, Noah watches with tears in his eyes, moved by the milestone she has reached. After all the questions and uncertainty surrounding her conversion, the moment marks a major turning point for the couple. Rabbi Eden jokes that the next step is for Noah and Joanne to start having kids as they build their Jewish family.

As if the engagement wasn’t enough of a surprise, Noah and Joanne take their relationship one step further in the season three finale: They get married! After Joanne completes her conversion, the couple reflects on the sacred moment they’ve just shared. But as drama between their families reaches a boiling point — particularly Morgan’s inability to be in the same room as Sasha and Noah’s mother trying to control their wedding plans — they realize they’ve lost sight of what matters most: each other.

Instead of continuing to plan a wedding amid the family tension, Noah asks Rabbi Eden to marry them right there on the beach. Joanne agrees to the spontaneous idea, and they find a stranger walking his dog who happens to be Jewish and can serve as their witness. With Rabbi Eden officiating, Noah and Joanne tie the knot in an intimate beach ceremony, becoming Mr. and Mrs. Roklov.

All 10 episodes Nobody Wants This season three are now streaming on Netflix. Read all of THR’s coverage here.

#567. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy speaks at EU summit amid spat with Donald Trump

EU leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine at the Brussels summit. But souring relations with the US over Russia and Starlink and a big hole in the budget will make for a difficult winter for Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was applauded by EU leaders when he appeared at this week's summit in Brussels. But getting what he needs from Europe will be tough, and a public dispute with US President Donald Trump has put him in a very difficult position.

Speaking to press at the summit, he said that "Putin wants to destroy us" and that Ukraine must prepare for a hard winter.

Experts view the upcoming cold season as a rough one for Ukraine as well.

"Ukraine is arguably entering the most difficult winter since [Russia's] full scale invasion," Olena Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, a nonpartisan think-tank, told DW.

Three painful topics were on the table at the summit for discussion between Zelenskyy and EU leaders: US relations with Russia, Starlink ― and money.

Zelenskyy's visit to Brussels comes at a time when he needs European support more than ever. That's because his relationship with the US is worsening. Worries are growing in the EU and Ukraine that the US is growing more sympathetic to Russia.

President Trump told US news channel Newsmax: "I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin."

Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel on October 12, which signifies a step back from sanctions placed on Russia and a blow for Ukraine.

When Zelenskyy ordered Ukrainian forces to conduct fresh strikes on Russia's oil refineries, Trump labelled the Ukrainian leader's decision as "a disgrace."

At the press conference at the summit on Friday, Zelenskyy told reporters that he knows that US-built missiles "are being sent to the Middle East, so it is no secret that we are not a priority."

He is asking Europe instead to supply the military power Ukraine needs to get through the winter.

Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the US has been the biggest military donor to Ukraine. But the relationship between the two countries has become more difficult since the start of Donald Trump's second term in the White House.

Ukraine uses Starlink, a satellite Internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The country also uses Starshield, the military-grade version, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones, though not for long-range strikes in Russia.

At the summit, Zelenskyy spoke of his "deep and unpleasant" surprise upon finding out that Ukraine was experiencing disruptions to the systems. He said this has hobbled Ukraine's ability to defend itself.

Both Elon Musk and the White House say they are not responsible for the slowdown.

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the press at the summit before the talks began: "Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in [the] short term Europe can't replace this capability."

Prokopenko said that this was the reason "why Ukraine's most credible medium-term solution here is to continue relying on the US. And the EU is critical in this context in terms of backing Ukraine's requests for the US administration to keep those technologies on offer" for Kyiv.

Speaking to journalists at the summit, Zelenskyy said the speed of Starlink had still not been fully restored but had improved. He said Ukraine is cooperating with various countries, including France, to search for a partial solution.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy urged EU leaders Friday to keep backing Kyiv financially as well, asking for nearly $80 billion (€70 billion) more next year.

"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support," Zelenskyy said. "It will help us hold Russia back."

The EU gave Kyiv an approximately $100 billion (€90 billion) loan last year, making the EU Ukraine's biggest international backer. But the Ukrainian government is saying it needs more.

"The war is becoming objectively more expensive, and the Ukrainian economy is increasingly affected by the Russian strikes, leading to a drastic decline in tax and customs revenues," Prokopenko said. "So the needs will continue growing."

So will Ukraine get what it needs? Closing the summit, President of the European Council Antonio Costa said that Ukraine "remains a priority" and asked the European Commission to come up with a proposal to pull together more funds for the country in 2027.

Essentially, it looks as though the EU will try to find a way to meet Ukraine's cash demands ― though it is not yet clear how.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU will "continue to lead" but urged international partners to step up as well.

Zelenskyy will leave Brussels without concrete promises or numbers, but with renewed commitments for support from Europe.

The Ukrainian president concluded his press conference with an emotional statement: "We will keep living and fighting with dignity."

Victor Glover recalls how a suspected cabin leak warning came just 15 minutes before a crucial engine burn — and why receiving it just five minutes later could have changed everything.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — NASA's Artemis II astronauts were just minutes away from a critical engine burn that would send them toward the moon when an unexpected cabin leak warning threatened to change the course of their historic mission.

"If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn," Artemis II pilot Victor Glover revealed during an Oct. 18 discussion with Canadian former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival here in Tenerife.

The incident unfolded on April 2, the second day of the Artemis II mission, as the astronauts' Orion spacecraft swooped back toward Earth after traveling some 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) away. Orion had been completing a highly elliptical orbit around Earth, giving the crew and mission control an opportunity to test the capsule's systems before committing to the journey to the moon. Orion was now approaching its closest point to our planet, roughly 100 miles (160 km) above the surface, ahead of the crucial translunar injection (TLI) burn that would send the astronauts moonward.

"Jeremy looks out the window and says, 'I think we're going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,'" Glover recalled, referring to Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency. "Because we were getting so low."

The close approach brought additional challenges, as Orion passed through a region populated by orbital debris and satellites.

"The density of things is going up from where we are, and also an increase in radiation," Glover explained.

It was at this particularly demanding point in the mission that Orion issued a warning that indicated a possible cabin leak, around 15 minutes before the critical TLI burn.

"So, determining whether it was real or not was a big deal," Glover said.

The crew and mission control faced a crucial question: Was it safe to continue heading to the moon, or would they have to abandon the planned maneuver and cut the mission very short? "Are we going to do a TLI and burn to go to the moon, or are we putting on our spacesuits to prepare to come back to Earth right now?" Glover recalled.

The timing was particularly critical. The TLI burn was designed to propel Orion out of Earth orbit and onto its trajectory around the moon, marking the first time astronauts had headed toward Earth's nearest neighbor since the Apollo era.

Luckily, as NASA flight director Judd Frieling told us during an April 2 media briefing, the warning turned out to be a false alarm.

So Artemis II received the go-ahead. Orion fired its main engine for approximately five minutes and 50 seconds, successfully setting the four astronauts on their journey around the moon.

"We're watching the timer count down, velocities go up, and the magenta and green numbers coming together," Glover recalled.

"Everything is tracking. It's looking good."

Before long, the crew had broken free of Earth's gravitational hold and were hurtling toward the moon at around 24,500 mph (39,430 kph).

Despite the tense moments before the burn, Artemis II went on to make history. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (the mission's commander), Glover (pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist), along with Hansen, traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them, reaching a maximum distance of 252,756 miles (406,771 km) during their journey around the moon.

The four astronauts returned safely to Earth on April 10, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego after nearly 10 days in space.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#569. This Startup Is All In on Recursive Self-Improvement. Its Latest Model Is Scary Good

For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement, or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer.

Flint is the first offering from Recursive, a company that aims to use RSI to advance both AI itself and other areas of science using AI. “Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI,” Recursive CEO and cofounder Richard Socher told me.

Socher says his company used its recursive AI system, dubbed the Eureka Machine, to automate most elements of the model’s development. This enabled a company with a handful of researchers to build a world-class model in just a few months, he says.

Socher told me that the Eureka Machine devised a number of innovations, including a new way of training the base model, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon chips. Recursive shared benchmark scores that suggest Flint outperforms other models of similar size and architecture on coding tasks.

AI is already widely used to help build, test, and improve AI thanks to its amazing coding skills. This can speed up the process of refining a model and testing new ideas without the need for as much input from humans.

It is also possible to create a loop through which AI decides what improvements to make and then begins another round of improvement. For the moment this technique is limited, but if AI can contribute to every aspect of model development, then the process could theoretically continue indefinitely.

Some experts worry that letting AI improve itself in this manner could ultimately lead to disaster. These doomsayers claim that AI capable of improving indefinitely could escape human control and might decide that humans are an impediment to its goals.

Those concerns gained wider notice this September when a researcher quit Anthropic and warned that advances in AI, including recursive self-improvement, could lead to human extinction within a few years—a concern then echoed by a number of other experts. The idea of RSI has become so controversial that several bills in Congress propose to ban it.

Recursive sees these fears as more sci-fi than reality and believes legislation to prevent RSI is an unnecessary impediment to progress.

Socher says Flint was built using a system incapable of escaping human control. He says the goal is for the Eureka Machine itself to achieve full recursive self-improvement, but this would still be overseen by humans who could stop the process if it goes awry. “We hope that this shows people that indeed we have all the steps in place” to build such a system, he says.

Recursive has raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation from Google Ventures, Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Socher was previously the chief scientist at Salesforce, and his cofounders include Jeff Clune, a professor at the University of British Columbia who researches ways of building AI systems capable of learning indefinitely.

I must say I am impressed with Flint. I tested it on a Mac with 48 GB of RAM—a healthy amount but only enough to run a modest-size AI model like Flint, which has 40 billion parameters. The biggest models out there have several trillions of parameters, and they can only run on racks of industrial servers.

I used Flint to build a bunch of programs and found it to be both fast and very capable. In my experience, models of this size can be annoyingly error-prone or slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed my coding requests every time. I used it to create a command line to-do list, then tried having it build a program that scours the web for interesting research related to recursive self-improvement. I also had Flint whip up a simple website that explains how RSI works. You can see that here.

It’s unclear how much progress other US labs have made chasing recursive self-improvement, but some published work suggests fully recursive systems are already feasible. A team from Microsoft, Carnegie Mellon University, and the University of Virginia recently published work, for instance, showing how an AI coding agent can recursively improve itself by modifying the software harness that turns reasoning into useful action and its own model’s weights.

Perhaps there are risks to full RSI if you are close to building a godlike intelligence, but for the time being it seems like a very promising way to improve your own AI models. This is something I’ve dabbled with in previous editions of AI Lab.

Indeed, Socher says the approach used to build Flint could make cutting-edge AI more accessible. “It's the only way this very small team can produce a model that's actually better than any other model in its class,” he told me. “This will hopefully show people that [recursive self-improvement] is actually quite nice and will benefit a lot of people.”

#570. Noel Gallagher Says ‘F—‘ Vegetarians on ‘Chicken Shop Date’ — With One Very Notable Exception

The Oasis guitarist also recalled how meeting Matthew McConaughey inspired a change in his home decor.

Noel Gallagher, as is his nature, had some blunt words for non-meat-eaters while guesting on the Chicken Shop Date episode posted Friday (Oct. 23).

When asked at the start by host Amelia Dimoldenberg whether he liked chicken nuggets, the Oasis legend replied, “Who doesn’t?”

After she pointed out that vegetarians, by definition, aren’t fans of the delicacy, Gallagher said gravely: “F— those guys.”

“Worse,” he added when Dimoldenberg then brought up vegans. “No stamina.”

That said, the rocker did reconsider his hard-and-fast stance on the matter when Sir Paul McCartney came up. “He’s one of those rare people that when you meet them and walk away, you feel more good about yourself,” Gallagher gushed.

Dimoldenberg then noted that the former Beatle also looks and acts much younger than you’d expect from a person in their 80s. “Well, he’s vegetarian, eh?” the Manchester native conceded. “Must be something in it.”

Another person that Gallagher was thrilled to meet was Matthew McConaughey, according to the musician. Elsewhere in the Chicken Shop Date appearance, he revealed how he loved interacting with the actor so much, it inspired him to make a very specific purchase and switch up the decor at the entrance of his home.

“I’d met him at a friend’s wedding,” Gallagher shared. “I’d never met anyone like him, and I bought a life-sized cardboard cut-out and put it in the front window for a month.”

Those are just two of the many fun facts the sardonic rock star shared in his chat with Dimoldenberg, which also spanned Oasis’ massive stadium tour in 2025 and the band’s plans to embark on another trek next year. #571. Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars

A journey to Mars may be less challenging for the human heart than scientists once feared. A new study suggests that astronauts can adapt remarkably well to months of weightlessness, offering encouraging evidence that humans could endure the long trip to the Red Planet and function under its weaker gravity.

Researchers from Northwestern Medicine, UT Southwestern, and UT Houston monitored the hearts of 13 astronauts who spent approximately six months aboard the International Space Station. Their findings showed that although spaceflight initially affected heart performance, the astronauts gradually adapted, with intensive daily exercise playing an important role in maintaining their cardiovascular health.

One of NASA's major concerns about sending humans to Mars is how astronauts' hearts and circulatory systems will respond when they leave the weightless conditions of spaceflight (known as microgravity) and encounter Martian gravity, which is only about one-third as strong as Earth's.

Encouragingly, the researchers found that the astronauts showed no significant signs of cardiovascular strain when exposed to simulated Martian gravity after returning to Earth.

"With our findings, there is now reason to think that we would be able to traverse to Mars, get there and actually work on the surface of Mars," said study senior author Dr. James Thomas, professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

The study, published last month in the journal Circulation, is the first to investigate how the heart responds to simulated Martian gravity following an extended period in space.

How Daily Exercise Protects Astronauts' Hearts in Space

Living without gravity creates unusual challenges for the human body. On Earth, the heart constantly works against gravity to circulate blood, while muscles must support the body's weight. In space, those demands decrease substantially, allowing muscles and even the heart itself to shrink over time.

Returning to a gravitational environment can also be difficult. Astronauts on previous missions have frequently experienced dizziness or lightheadedness when standing after landing. This happens because gravity pulls blood toward the lower body, sometimes causing blood pressure to drop suddenly. The condition is called orthostatic hypotension. (If you've seen Sandra Bullock crawling after returning to Earth in "Gravity," you get the idea.)

However, the astronauts involved in the new study generally handled this transition well, potentially because they had maintained demanding exercise schedules throughout their missions.

As part of NASA's Exercise Countermeasures program, astronauts exercised for up to two hours each day. Their routines included 30 to 45 minutes of endurance training, which strengthens the cardiovascular system, along with 60 to 75 minutes of resistance training to help preserve muscle mass and strength.

"You lose muscle mass and cardiac mass when you're in a weightless environment because you are working less up there," explained Thomas, who also is a Northwestern Medicine cardiologist. "You're floating around in the air, and you give a little tap with your foot, and you can sail over to say hello to your buddy."

"To counter that, exercise is crucial when you're in space," Thomas added.

Heart Scans Reveal How the Body Adapts to Weightlessness

To understand what happens to the heart during prolonged spaceflight, the researchers collected echocardiograms before, during, and after each astronaut's mission. These ultrasound scans use sound waves to produce moving images of the heart, allowing doctors to examine its structure and measure how effectively it pumps blood.

While aboard the International Space Station, astronauts were trained to perform these scans on one another every few weeks. The recordings were transmitted to Earth, where researchers could monitor changes in heart function throughout the missions.

Thomas worked alongside Dr. Benjamin Levine of UT Southwestern Medical Center and Dr. Michael Bungo of the McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.

"It would be typically about 3 a.m. for me because the space station runs on Greenwich Mean Time," Thomas said. "I would watch the recordings come in live and coach the astronauts in real time to improve the images."

The scans revealed that the astronauts' hearts initially struggled to adjust to their new environment. During the first two weeks in space, researchers observed declines in cardiac filling, stroke volume, and several other measures of cardiovascular performance.

Cardiac filling refers to how much blood enters the heart between beats, while stroke volume describes the amount of blood pumped out with each contraction. Both measurements decreased early in the missions, indicating that the astronauts' hearts were temporarily moving less blood with each beat.

As the astronauts spent more time in space, their cardiovascular systems adapted. Cardiac filling and stroke volume gradually improved, approaching the levels recorded before launch.

These results suggest that the heart can adjust to prolonged weightlessness more effectively than early measurements might indicate, particularly when astronauts maintain regular physical activity.

Astronauts' Hearts Pass a Simulated Mars Gravity Test

The researchers also wanted to answer a particularly important question for future Mars missions: What happens when an astronaut who has spent months in weightlessness suddenly encounters gravity again?

Mars has roughly 38% of Earth's surface gravity. Although this is considerably weaker than what people experience on Earth, it would still force astronauts' hearts to work differently after months of floating in space.

To reproduce some of these effects, the researchers conducted a simulated Martian gravity test after the astronauts returned to Earth.

Each astronaut was tilted upward by 22 degrees from a lying position. This posture caused blood to shift toward the lower body, approximating the circulatory effects of Martian gravity.

The results were encouraging. After spending about six months in space, the astronauts' hearts performed just as well under simulated Martian gravity as they had when standing upright on Earth before their missions.

This suggests that astronauts who maintain their cardiovascular fitness during spaceflight may be capable of transitioning to the weaker gravity of Mars without experiencing major cardiovascular difficulties.

Although the findings come from a relatively small group of astronauts and a simulation rather than an actual Mars landing, they provide valuable evidence for planning future missions.

Combined with the benefits of daily exercise, the heart's ability to adapt to weightlessness and respond well to simulated Martian gravity offers another reason to be optimistic about sending humans to the Red Planet.

The study is titled "Impact of Prolonged Spaceflight on Cardiac Structure and Function: An Exploratory Longitudinal Observational Study." Funding was provided by the National Space Biomedical Research Institute (grant NCC9-58), NASA (grant NNJ04HH01A), the IDP Foundation, Sandra Helton, and the National Heart Foundation of Australia.

#572. Holland Taylor Reveals Why She Left Two and a Half Men Contract

Actress Holland Taylor explained why she didn't want to renew her contract with Two and a Half Men after six years, preferring to return only as a guest star on the Charlie Sheen and Jon Cryer show.

Holland Taylor is giving her two and a half cents on being underpaid.

The Two and a Half Men actress—who played Evelyn Harper, the mother of Charlie (Charlie Sheen) and Alan (Jon Cryer) on the CBS show—revealed why she didn't renew her contract after six years, instead opting to return occasionally as a guest star.

“I stopped being under contract. So, in other words, they would say, ‘Can you do a guest appearance at the end of March?’ And I would say, ‘No, I cannot,'” Taylor said on the Oct. 21 episode of Alchemy with Anthony Mason. "I only did it if I wanted to do it."

Though the 83-year-old said the producers were "astonished" by her choice, she appreciated the flexibility in scheduling. Plus, she noted that her paycheck wasn't as big as she would have liked.

"They never paid me very well on that show. I was paid on that show what I had made on a series like eight years before or something," she said. “And I got four Emmy nominations and they never gave me a raise. They usually do.”

“I loved a lot about that show, but they were not full of courtesies,” Taylor continued. “In any case, when the six years was up, I said, ‘I don’t want to be on a contract anymore but I will visit the show occasionally if you want.’ I mean, I did play the boys’ mother.”

The Legally Blonde star explained that the Two and a Half Men team thought she was negotiating, telling her, "We can't pay you any more money."

"I said, 'You could actually pay me the cost of this building, but don't bother because I don't want to continue on under contract,'" she retorted. "And they said, 'But we can't afford to give you more.' I said, 'I'm cool with it. I just will come back as a guest from time to time.'"

And of course, it wasn't the only shakeup in the cast. Sheen left the show in 2011 following public struggles with substance abuse and Ashton Kutcher entered as billionaire Walden Schmidt in the later seasons.

To see what the cast is up to now, read on.

Charlie Sheen—the son of Martin Sheen and brother to Emilio Estevez—was one of the original "men" in Two and a Half Men, playing Charlie Harper in the first eight seasons of the CBS sitcom opposite on-screen brother Jon Cryer. The eighth season was cut short in 2011 amid Sheen's battle with addiction.He famously clashed with executive producer Chuck Lorre in the press and social media, resulting in his dismissal from the series (and the coinage of phrases like "winning" and "tiger blood"). His character was killed off and later played as a ghost by Kathy Bates.After exiting Two and a Half Men, Sheen booked the TV version of Anger Management, which aired from 2012 to 2014. Since, he popped up on The Goldbergs and on the big screen in Scary Movie 5, Machete Kills and 9/11.

In 2023, the actor—who shared in 2015 he is HIV-positive—made a cameo as himself on Lorre's Max series Bookies. He released his memoir The Book of Sheen as well as the two-part documentary aka Charlie Sheen in 2025.Sheen, who revealed in 2015 that he is HIV-positive, has been sober since late 2017. He shares sons Bob Sheen and Max Sheen with ex-wife Brooke Mueller, daughters Sami Sheen and Lola Sheen with ex-wife Denise Richards and daughter Cassandra Estevez from a previous relationship.

Cryer starred in all 12 seasons of Two and a Half Men as Charlie's divorcee brother Alan Harper.After the show, Cryer released a 2015 memoir and popped up on shows like Mom, The Ranch, NCIS, Robot Chicken and Lady Dynamite. Cryer then went on to play Lex Luthor on the TV series Supergirl from 2019 to 2021 as well as Jim Kearney on Extended Family, which ran from 2023 to 2024.Cryer shares daughter Daisy with wife Lisa Joyner as well as son Charlie with ex-wife Sarah Trigger.Though Cryer agreed to sit down for Netflix's aka Charlie Sheen, the two aren’t exactly friends. "We don’t have a relationship anymore," Cryer said on a January 2025 episode of Club Random With Bill Maher. "I wish him the best. We have some mutual friends still, and I’ve heard he’s been sober for a while, which is great to hear."

Angus T. Jones played the "half man" in Two and a Half Men, starring as Jake, Alan Harper's son. He became the highest paid child actor on TV at age 17, but then left the series in 2013 after forging down a religious path. However, he did return for the series finale in 2015.Jones attended University of Colorado Boulder after leaving the sitcom and, at one point, teamed up with Sean Combs' son Justin Combs for a media and events company.In 2023, he made a cameo as himself on Lorre's Max series Bookies. Jones continues to lead a life out of the spotlight, but noted in a 2020 Instagram post, "I do music now, go head and get used to it loves."

That 70s Show alum Ashton Kutcher joined Two and a Half Men in season nine after Sheen's infamous exit and stayed through the end of the series in 2015. He played billionaire Walter Schmidt, who purchased Charlie Harper's house following the character's death.

After Two and a Half Men wrapped, Kutcher appeared on shows like The Ranch as well as in movies like Vengeance and Your Place or Mine. He's also a venture capitalist, having invested in companies like Airbnb and Uber. Kutcher married his costar from That '70s Show Mila Kunis months after the series wrapped in July 2015. The married duo are parents to daughter Wyatt and son Dimitri.

Conchata Ferrell popped up in supporting roles throughout her career, including Erin Brockovich, Network, L.A. Law and E/R (not to be confused with ER). As wisecracking housekeeper Berta on Two and a Half Men, she received two Emmy nominations.

After Men ended, Ferrell appeared in Krampus, Grace and Frankie and reunited with Kutcher on The Ranch. She died in October 2020 at 77 years old.

After the CBS sitcom ended, Marin Hinkle—who played Alan's ex-wife Judith— appeared in Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle on the big screen, and as part of The Affair, Red Band Society, Madam Secretary, Homeland and Speechless on the small. She then landed the role of Rose Weissman on The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, which ran from 2017 to 2023. Hinkle shares son Ben with her ex-husband Randall Sommer.

Melanie Lynskey is best known to Two and a Half Men fans as Rose, the Harper's kinda strange next-door neighbor. After having a relationship with Charlie, she claimed in season nine that he had died. But in the series finale, it was revealed she kept him prisoner for four years.

Lynskey is known for her roles in films like Sadie, Little Boxes, The Changeover and Pike River, plus her TV performances in shows like Togetherness, Castle Rock, Mrs. America, Candy and Yellowjackets. Lynskey welcomed a daughter with Jason Ritter in 2018, and the couple wed two years later.

Amber Tamblyn joined the cast for seasons 11 and 12 as Jenny, Charlie's long-lost illegitimate daughter.Since the end of Two and a Half Men, the Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants alum has appeared in You Hurt My Feelings, Y: The Last Man, Nostalgia, and Girlfriend's Day. She also directed and co-wrote the 2016 film Paint It Black.Tamblyn wed David Cross in 2012 and they welcomed daughter Marlow five years later.

Holland Taylor starred in all 12 seasons of Two and a Half Men as Evelyn, Alan and Charlie's mother.Afterwards, The Practice alum appeared in several more TV shows, including The Morning Show, The Chair, Hollywood, and Mr. Mercedes. Her list of film credits has also grown to include Motherland, Quiz Lady, The Stand In, Bombshell and Gloria Bell.Taylor has been in a relationship with Sarah Paulson since 2015.

#573. Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing at training

Kompany was appointed Bayern Munich manager in May 2024

Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing as he watched the club's second team train on Friday.

The 40-year-old had been unwell with a virus and missed the pre-match news conference on Tuesday prior to Bayern's Champions League game against Arsenal.

The former Manchester City and Belgium defender was subsequently on the touchline for the match on Wednesday.

Reports in Germany say Kompany is in a stable condition in hospital.

"Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during an FC Bayern reserve team training session on Friday," said a statement from the Bundesliga club., external

"The first-team head coach was watching the second string's session.

"Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations in hospital and will remain under medical care.

"His coaching staff will oversee training and match activities until further notice."

Bayern's next game is against Freiburg in the German top flight on Sunday.

"Vincent Kompany's health is our top priority. We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure his speedy recovery," said Bayern sporting director Max Eberl.

"Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, and all the time he needs.

"His coaching team, in whom we have complete confidence, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery."

Aaron Danks, one of Kompany's assistants, took the pre-match news conference for Bayern before the Arsenal game.

German football journalist Taufig Khalil told BBC Radio 5 Live that Kompany had been "suffering with the virus for about a week".

He added: "The thing started last weekend on Saturday against Leipzig, and that's the first time we saw Vincent Kompany [when] he didn't look very well.

"He didn't do the press conference after, and Max Eberl told us that he's suffering with a virus.

"Everybody was really surprised that Vincent Kompany was standing there with his black jacket in the pouring rain of Munich on Wednesday night against Arsenal. Everybody expected Aaron Danks to be there.

"The problem was that maybe you couldn't bench Vincent Kompany, the game was too important for him.

"Bayern Munich just told us that he's in stable conditions. There was a helicopter involved in the whole thing, which landed on the training ground at Bayern Munich, but he was not brought into the hospital by helicopter. They brought him with a medical car and he will be now there."

Kompany left his role as Burnley manager to take over at Bayern in May 2024, succeeding current England manager Thomas Tuchel.

He had won the Championship with Burnley in 2022-23 and, despite the Clarets being relegated from the Premier League under him the following season, Kompany was appointed by the Bundesliga club.

He has led Bayern to the German top-flight title in the past two seasons and reached the 2025-26 Champions League semi-finals before being beaten by eventual winners Paris St-Germain.

Kompany spent 11 years at Manchester City as a player, winning four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and four League Cups.

"Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and club legend, Vincent Kompany," said City in a post on social media. "Get well soon, Vinny."

"Everyone here at Burnley FC sends our best wishes to Vincent and we wish him a speedy recovery," said a Burnley statement.
