#575. Hijab ban at schools in Azerbaijan: What's behind the rare wave of protests?

Girls wearing headscarves have been turned away from schools in Azerbaijan, triggering unusual protests involving children. The government rules do not mention hijabs. Why are schools enforcing unwritten rules?

A dispute over Islamic headscarves in Azerbaijani schools has triggered protests at home and an unusual exchange of criticism between politicians in Azerbaijan and Turkey, two countries whose leaders routinely describe their relationship as that of "one nation, two states". The row has raised questions about religious freedom, sovereignty and the limits of Turkish and Iranian influence in the south Caucasian country.

The unprecedented protests have been taking place across Azerbaijan for a nearly week. Children have demonstrated against the headscarf ban introduced at schools. Among those rallying outside of schools are girls who wear Islamic headscarves; others, including boys, have joined classmates in solidarity.

Rallies in general are rare in a country where police routinely disperse any public protests. But demonstrations involving children are unprecedented in Azerbaijan. As the videos showing the protests started spreading on social media, access to Instagram and TikTok was disrupted in the country, indicating how seriously the authorities are taking the issue. Internet monitors documented blocks; the authorities have not explained their cause.

The dispute follows a series of legal changes. On July 7, Azerbaijan amended its general education law, reinforcing the principle of secular education and requiring pupils and teachers to comply with dress codes. On September 21, the government adopted Resolution No. 309, tightening school uniform rules.

The resolution prohibits additional clothing that disrupts the standard uniform or conflicts with secular education. It does not explicitly mention the hijab ― a Muslim headscarf covering the hair and neck ― or instruct schools to exclude pupils wearing one. But some school administrators have interpreted the rule as applying to hijabs and turned girls covering their heads away. The regulation gives each school's pedagogical council responsibility for resolving compliance issues.

A separate decision on October 6 set dress requirements for teachers. Reports followed of women wearing headscarves being prevented from teaching.

Azerbaijan is a predominantly Muslim country, but Article 18 of its constitution separates religion from the state and requires state education to be secular. Articles 42 and 48 protect the right to education and freedom of conscience.

Supporters of the schools' actions say the same dress rules should apply to all pupils. Critics argue that excluding girls because of religious clothing violates their rights. The dispute cuts across conventional political divisions: some government critics support the restrictions, while some non-religious Azerbaijanis oppose them. School headscarf restrictions also prompted protests in 2010 and subsequent years.

A Baku literature teacher with 40 years of experience, said that girls wearing headscarves were not admitted to classes at the teacher's school. Some removed their scarves; others went home or wanted to study at home. The teacher, who didn't want to be identified by name and provided only the initials M.C., supported enforcing the uniform rules, arguing that children were too young to make decisions about religious dress.

A parent identified as D.A. told DW this was not a nationwide hijab ban, but a matter of school uniforms. Another parent who opposed the restrictions withdrew an interview before publication.

Facebook user Sarraf Cabbarov from Baku posted on his social media account that his daughter Sevil, a primary school teacher in Azerbaijan's capital, was dismissed for refusing to remove her headscarf. He also published a school order issuing her a written warning under the new dress regulations.

On October 12, the Interior Ministry said 37 people had been detained in connection with the protests. According to the ministry's statement, the group had confronted school staff, damaged property and attempted to obstruct school activities and traffic. A criminal case was opened under Article 233, concerning disruption of public order. The ministry did not identify those detained or say whether they included children.

Artist and activist Ilkin Huseynov went missing after launching a project linking volunteer tutors with pupils affected by the restrictions. Local media later reported, citing people close to him, that he had been given 30 days of administrative detention for allegedly disobeying police orders.

Some observers linked the introduction of the new rules for school uniform to the attempts by the Azerbaijani government to counter the influence of neighboring Iran and the growing strength of religious groups within the country. This interpretation is, in essence, echoed by government officials as well, although they stop short of explicitly naming Iran.

Fazil Mustafa, who chairs the Committee for Public Associations and Religious Institutions at Azerbaijan's parliament, said the authorities were concerned about religious groups influenced from abroad and defended the school rules. Allahshukur Pashazade, head of the Caucasus Muslims Office, also warned of outside interference but called for a peaceful solution. The alleged foreign involvement has not been independently established.

Amnesty International condemned the exclusion of girls wearing hijabs and called for the release of anyone detained solely for protesting peacefully.

The controversy has also drawn criticism in Turkey, Azerbaijan's close ally. Protesters gathered outside Azerbaijan's consulate in Istanbul on October 3. Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, criticized the restrictions,saying it's unacceptable to deny education to students wearing headscarves. Azerbaijan's ruling New Azerbaijan Party replied that close relations did not justify interference in its internal affairs.

For affected families, the immediate question remains whether children can attend school without removing their headscarves.

#576. Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers

Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics, AI agents, and modular data centers, with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.

“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.”

The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face—doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch.

Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said.

The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out.

Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs.

Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said.

On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data.

He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher.

In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair.

#577. Vince Gill & Charlie Handsome Lead 2026 NMPA Gold & Platinum Gala Honorees

The 2026 National Music Publishers' Association Gold & Platinum Gala, held Thursday, honored over 150 Nashville songwriters.

The National Music Publishers’ Association celebrated an array of top country songs and the writers who created them Thursday night (Oct. 22), during the 8th annual NMPA Gold and Platinum Gala, held at the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum in downtown Nashville.

The NMPA’s president/CEO David Israelite welcomed the audience of songwriters, music publishers and others in Nashville’s music industry elite, while the company’s Cara Cunningham and Charlotte Sellmyer were among those also leading the charge in honoring writers. Related Tate McRae Debuts at No. 1 In Australia With 'Housewife' Lars Brandle

The event honored over 150 songwriters whose country songs have achieved Gold, Platinum, Multi-Platinum and Diamond or above status, as certified by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) from the July 2025-June 2026 eligibility period. Songwriting plaques were presented to more than 80 multi-platinum hitmakers from the Nashville community.

Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) CEO Mitch Glazier was also in attendance to honor the hits and songwriters recognized during the ceremony.

Laci Kaye Booth launched the evening with a performance of her song “Daddy’s Mugshot,” featured on her new album Love Ain’t for the Faint of Heart.

The annual NMPA Gold and Platinum Gala honors new RIAA certifications for songs, no matter when they were initially released; thus, the evening feted songs both new and classic. Numerous songs were honored during the evening, including the Morgan Wallen-recorded “Chasing You,” which was celebrated Diamond, the Carrie Underwood-recorded “Before He Cheats” (11x Platinum), and a handful of 12x-Platinum songs: Shaboozey’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy),” Combs’s “Hurricane” and Wallen’s “Last Night,” as well as his 13x-Platinum “Whiskey Glasses.”

Also among the songs honored this year was the 3x Platinum “Jesus, Take the Wheel,” written by Gordie Sampson, Hillary Lindsey, and the late Brett James. Cornman Music president Nate Lowery accepted the accolade on behalf of James, who passed away just over a year ago. The audience responded with tremendous applause and a standing ovation.

The platinum anthem honor, which recognizes the highest-certified song of the year, went to “Beautiful Crazy,” written by Luke Combs, Rob Williford and Wyatt Durrette, and recorded by Combs. The song earned 15x Platinum certification in December 2025. Brett Young honored the writers by putting his own soulful spin on a performance of “Beautiful Crazy,” while songwriter Williford took the stage to accept the honor.

“I think about that kid that just dreamed about hearing a song he wrote on the radio,” Williford said. “I thought, ‘Man, if I can just accomplish that, if I got a No. 1, or if I won song of the year, I will have made it. I’m here to tell you, I’m here 10 years later, and I’m just as hungry, just as fired up, I’m still trying to chase this passion of pulling lyric and melody out of thin air.”

Charlie Handsome was celebrated as top songwriter of the year. It was noted that he earned 35 new RIAA certifications over the last year, in the country genre alone. Among his certified songs being honored were “Wasted on You,” “Last Night,” “You Proof” and “Heartless.”

“Thanks everybody who helped,” Handsome told the crowd. “I want to thank my family – my mom’s here, my brother, my wife. All the guys I write with… it’s the same crew every time but without them I’m not here.”

Vince Gill was honored with the legacy songwriter icon award, for his work in writing lasting impactful hits. His songs “One More Last Chance” and “Go Rest High on That Mountain” received new certifications.

“His awards are countless, his talent is extraordinary, his humility is legendary,” Israelite told the audience. “But perhaps his greatest achievement is that, after all these years, his songs aren’t just standing the test of time — they are making history.”

“I love writing songs, always have,” Gill told the audience. “It kind of came last, the songs did…I was always known for my singing, always known for my guitar playing, stuff like that… took a while for people to believe I was a decent songwriter. I sure was grateful for that change.”

Gill then shared the often-told story of how the late Country Music Hall of Famer George Jones once drove a riding lawn mower several miles to purchase alcohol, after his wife had hidden his car keys to prevent him from drinking; that tale helped inspire Gill’s 1992 song “One More Last Chance,” which he performed during the NMPA gala. Gill then also offered up perhaps the evening’s most moving moment, a version of his song “Go Rest High on That Mountain,” a song he said he wrote for his older brother.

“I’m grateful for this song and what it has gone on to do to help people get through a rough stretch,” Gill said.

Somewhere in the vast Western Australia wilderness lies a giant "spider" trapped in an ancient impact crater.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

From the dangerous Sydney funnel-web to the common huntsman, Australia is home to its fair share of spiders. It even has a crater shaped like one.

One stretch of the vast Western Australia wilderness is imprinted with a curious crater, which likely formed after a meteor impact hundreds of millions of years ago. Geologists think the spider-like pattern in the crater's center was created when its floor rebounded following the initial impact, NASA has said.

In the hundreds of millions of years since the initial impact, erosion has continued to carve this formation into its current, signature shape. Complete with "legs," the planetary imprint has earned its name Spider Crater.

This image shows the impact structure in its entirety, which stretches 8 by 7 miles (13 by 11 kilometers) in full, with the central "spider" piece measuring 2.5 miles (4 km).

In this image, we can see this "spider" from space. This snapshot shows the geologic feature as captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the Landsat 9 satellite, an Earth-observing craft that launched back in 2021.

The satellite, a collaborative effort between NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey, is the ninth in the Landsat Earth-observing series, which goes all the way back to the launch of Landsat 1 in 1972. On a near-weekly basis, Landsat 9 delivers observations of everything from deforestation to water quality and crop growth.

The series of Landsat satellites have been a critical piece in the modern understanding of how our planet continues to change. Whether it's the repercussions of climate change or fluctuations in agriculture, observations from orbit do more than provide interesting photos of our home world; they also capture critical data.

With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #579. I’m expected to work excessive hours in the lab. Should I speak up about my disability?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A few months ago, I started a PhD at a university in North America. I have a disability that affects both my physical and my mental capacity, and its impact on me fluctuates. The more I can rest, the fewer symptom flare-ups I experience.

Unfortunately, my laboratory has a severe problem with overwork. Most students work 50–60 hours a week and sometimes more. We’re constantly asked to take on new tasks for the projects of our principal investigator (PI), often with tight deadlines. I’ll go into the lab intending to work on my experiments and end up spending all day on my PI’s tasks.

My PI, to whom I have not disclosed my health status, has repeatedly expressed disappointment in my work ethic. I have worked in other labs with different supervisors without facing issues (during my master’s degree, for example), and I know I’m not the only person struggling in this environment: my lab-mates are also burnt out.

Many of my issues are tied to being unable to take breaks while working long hours, often 12–16 hours per day for several days in a row. In previous jobs in which my colleagues and I worked overtime, we could take the equivalent amount of time off either the following week or as holiday time. But in my current lab, we’re expected to come back to work immediately. Sometimes we’re called in on weekends. I can barely keep up because I’m given no time to rest. A task that would take me an hour now takes longer because I’m fighting through pain. When I asked for time off, I received a firm no.

I’m nervous about what I might face in the rest of my programme. I know that I can have the success I want if I find the right environment. I plan to seek accommodations by contacting someone at my university. But should I disclose to my PI? I fear it might make things worse, and that I will face disability stigma. What can I do to make sure myself and other students are well cared for and protected? — A disabled graduate student

“Disability stigma contributes to power imbalances between graduate students and advisers,” says Bonnielin Swenor, director of the Johns Hopkins Disability Health Research Center in Baltimore, Maryland. That stigma is evident from discrepancies in earnings1 and grant outcomes2 between disabled and non-disabled researchers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields, according to her research on US scientists. Understandably, then, “taking action can feel intimidating, and many disabled scientists fear retribution”, she says.

“What you describe is not a personal failure of work ethic,” emphasizes Deepti Sharma, a management researcher at Ahmedabad University in India. You’re in a dysfunctional work environment, in which “your disability made the dysfunction visible to you earlier and more painfully than it did for others”.

Nature’s careers team asked Sharma, Swenor and two other researchers for advice on how disabled graduate students and other people facing similar challenges can protect themselves.

Rebecca Williams, an environmental-law researcher and disability officer at the University of Glasgow, UK, says that there should be staff members who can offer support to students. She recommends investigating what resources are available at your university. These could be from a graduate-student union, a director of graduate studies or university disability services.

In many regions, there is a legal duty not to discriminate against people with disabilities, Williams adds. She also suggests checking whether your university offers any grants or other financial support for the resources that you might need. One source of guidance could be the Job Accommodation Network, a US website providing information on workplace accommodations.

Sharma distinguishes between formal and personal disclosure: “Registering with your university’s disability-services office is a formal, documented process that establishes the accommodations you are entitled to.” At most institutions, the office should inform supervisors only of the accommodations required, not the diagnoses that prompted them. “Personal disclosure to a PI is a separate, discretionary act,” says Sharma, who strongly encourages formal registration as a first step. “Regardless of what you decide about your PI, informal goodwill evaporates under pressure, while documented accommodations do not.”

Williams recommends pausing before deciding whether to approach your PI: “You may want to wait until you have a better sense of your new PI’s supervisory style before you decide how much or little you want to disclose beyond the accommodations that you need.”

To make best use of institutional resources, all four disability advocates stress the importance of documentation. “Keep written records such as e-mails confirming verbal instructions and notes on refused leave requests,” advises Sharma. “Patterns documented over time carry far more weight with a department than any single complaint.” Doing this could also help other students who face similar issues with your PI.

Swenor notes that “keeping detailed records of e-mails and interactions in which disability discrimination occurs is often necessary. As with any form of discrimination, this information provides the needed support if or when you choose to file a complaint or grievance,” she says. “It is also essential to understand your rights and legal protections.”

But, she cautions, keeping a record is only one step. “Formally documenting your needed accommodations does not eliminate bias or discrimination,” she says.

Sharma suggests “building a support structure outside your supervisor’s control: a thesis committee member you trust, a mentor in another department, peers in your cohort”. This support structure could include your head of department or, if it exists, a staff disability network that can connect you to supportive staff members or graduate students who might have relevant lived experience, says Williams.

“Disability in academia is often about finding ‘your people’, who understand what it is to manage health difficulties,” notes Williams, who has written about her own experiences of dealing with chronic illness in academia. “Sometimes finding people that ‘get it’ will help you feel less alone during the process of your PhD, and gauge what a realistic daily or weekly PhD routine might be for you.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02582-6

You might not expect the hunky thespian to be close with the dude from Superbad, but look at it this way: Brad is a total prankster (says Jonah) and Jonah is now a serious Oscar nominee (for their film Moneyball).

The controversial rapper joined forces with Sir Elton at the 2001 Grammys and later Em turned to his new friend for support getting sober: "I told him, 'Look, I'm going through a problem and I need your advice.'"

#581. Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells

Scientists in Germany have found a way to dramatically reverse the molecular age of human cells, transforming blood cells from an 80-year-old person into stem cells with an age signature of less than 20 years.

Researchers at the University Hospital of Bonn and the University of Bonn achieved this remarkable transformation by reprogramming immature red blood cells into neural stem cells, which can eventually develop into brain cells. During the process, molecular markers associated with aging were effectively reset, making the cells more than 60 years younger at the molecular level.

Unlike earlier approaches, the rejuvenation happened gradually, allowing scientists to follow the changes over an extended period. This slower process could provide important clues about how cellular aging can be reversed and potentially help researchers investigate treatments for diseases associated with aging.

The findings were published in the journal Aging Cell.

How Scientists Turn Blood Cells Into Brain Stem Cells

The human body contains hundreds of specialized cell types, all of which originate from a single fertilized egg and carry essentially the same genetic instructions. As cells develop, however, they take on specific roles. Under normal circumstances, a skin cell cannot transform into a liver cell, and a blood cell cannot become a nerve cell.

Modern laboratory techniques have made it possible to overcome these biological restrictions. Scientists can now reprogram certain mature cells to adopt entirely different identities. For example, skin cells can be converted into cells capable of producing nerve tissue, an approach that could eventually contribute to treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.

The process relies on a combination of proteins called transcription factors, which regulate how genes are activated. By changing which genetic instructions a cell follows, these proteins can redirect its development and give it a new cellular identity.

"Using this method, we have directly converted red blood cell precursors into neural stem cells," explains Prof. Dr. Oliver Brüstle, director of the Institute of Reconstructive Neurobiology at the University Hospital of Bonn.

Earlier experiments by the Bonn team had already demonstrated that nerve cells generated through this approach could successfully connect with existing neurons after being transplanted into the brains of mice.

Scientists Reverse More Than 60 Years of Cellular Aging

The latest investigation focused on an especially intriguing consequence of cellular reprogramming: the dramatic reversal of molecular aging.

"In our current study, however, we focused on a different phenomenon: namely, the observation that cells become significantly rejuvenated during reprogramming," emphasizes Brüstle, who is also a member of the Transdisciplinary Research Area (TRA) Life & Health at the University of Bonn.

To determine how much the cells had rejuvenated, the researchers examined their molecular clocks, particularly biological markers known as epigenetic clocks. These clocks estimate a cell's biological age by analyzing chemical modifications to DNA that tend to accumulate or change as organisms grow older.

Importantly, these modifications do not alter the DNA sequence itself. Instead, they affect how frequently certain genetic instructions are used (epigenetics). Because these patterns change predictably with age, scientists can use them to estimate how old a cell appears at the molecular level.

The results were striking. After reprogramming, cells taken from an 80-year-old individual displayed molecular age signatures corresponding to someone younger than 20. In other words, the process had reversed more than six decades of cellular aging.

"We also know that this epigenetic rejuvenation ensures that the cells actually behave like young cells," says the scientist.

A Slower Rejuvenation Process Reveals New Clues

Scientists have previously observed that reprogramming cells can reset their biological age. However, earlier demonstrations of this effect involved a more complicated process requiring two distinct stages.

First, researchers would convert an existing cell, such as a blood cell, into a pluripotent stem cell. These versatile cells have nearly unlimited developmental "career paths" because they can give rise to many different cell types throughout the body.

The pluripotent stem cell would then be guided into becoming a neural stem cell, which is more specialized and can produce cells found in the nervous system.

This conventional approach produces rejuvenation relatively quickly, making it difficult to examine all the changes taking place.

The Bonn researchers instead bypassed the pluripotent stage entirely.

"In contrast, we converted blood cells directly into neural stem cells -- that is, without first passing through the pluripotent cell stage," said Brüstle. "In our approach, rejuvenation occurred gradually and could be tracked for over 100 days."

The researchers observed a dramatic reduction in molecular age, with the study highlighting rejuvenation of approximately 60 years after 50 days. Because the process continued over a much longer period, scientists could examine the biological changes as they unfolded rather than observing only the final result.

What Cellular Rejuvenation Could Mean for Alzheimer's Research

The ability to watch cells gradually become younger could be particularly valuable for scientists trying to understand the mechanisms that control biological aging.

By studying this extended transformation, researchers can investigate which molecular pathways are involved and test whether particular substances can speed up or slow down the rejuvenation process.

"Rejuvenation that extends over such a long period of time is ideal as an experimental model: Since the epigenetic clocks are slowly reset over several weeks, we can use this model to investigate which factors and active substances accelerate or slow down the rejuvenation process."

The findings could be especially relevant to neuroscience, where aging is closely connected to the development of serious neurological conditions. Although the work does not establish a treatment capable of reversing aging in people, it offers a laboratory model for investigating how cells regain youthful characteristics.

This could eventually help scientists better understand the cellular changes associated with conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.

"After all, age is the most important risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's!"

The research involved teams from the University Hospital of Bonn, the University of Bonn, and RWTH Aachen University. Funding was provided by the EU's Horizon 2020 program, the German Research Foundation (DFG), and the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space (BMFRT).

#582. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#583. Carrick refuses to rule out dropping Fernandes in emotional address

Man Utd boss Carrick responds to criticism

Under-pressure Manchester United boss Michael Carrick delivered a passionate and emotional address lasting five minutes and 30 seconds as he battles to save his job.

And he refused to rule out dropping skipper Bruno Fernandes for Sunday's Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

Instead of taking his seat and answering questions as normal in Friday's scheduled pre-match media conference at Carrington, Carrick said he wanted to start himself.

It was a strategy former boss Sir Alex Ferguson used, although the legendary Scot rarely spoke at such length.

After a run of seven games without a win, culminating in Wednesday's shocking 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como, and attacks on the club's hierarchy by defender Lisandro Martinez and then Fernandes' condemnation of his own tactics in Italy, Carrick wanted to reaffirm his view of what United stood for.

"Recently we haven't had a good time, I think that's pretty obvious," he said.

"Wednesday was a bad night, and it hurt me to see us play like that. It was unacceptable.

"My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club, and the supporters, and they can be proud of in the identity we show. We have gone away from that recently. It's important we all recognise that.

"The foundation and values of this football club have been etched for many years. I totally understand and get every single one of them.

"There's a resilience about this football club that runs very deep. I've seen it with my own eyes, I've felt it, I'm know some of the individuals closely who have been a big part of that history.

"Entitlement cannot be at this football club.

"It was based on being humble, having humility, and hard work. We can never lose that, and I won't let us lose that."

Asked about Fernandes and whether he has considered dropping him, a defiant Carrick added: "The most important thing for me is the team, the squad and dynamics in the squad.

"It's about the football club. I'll always do what is best for the football club."

Conte plays down 'unfounded' Man Utd speculation

Should Man Utd boss Carrick drop captain Fernandes?

Have Man Utd become the unmanageable club?

Manchester United won 12 of their 17 games under Michael Carrick last season

Club sources said on Thursday Fernandes would not have the captaincy taken away or be fined for his post-match observations following the Como defeat.

In a further interview on Wednesday night with Sky Italia, the Portugal international referred to Manchester United's storied history.

"At this club, there's too much focus on what's been done in the past," said Fernandes. "But we're not those people anymore. The club and the players need to understand that.

"Unfortunately for us - especially when it comes to the players - those who join expect to win trophies, win games, and reach the highest level, that's been very difficult at this club in recent years."

Whether Carrick was aware of Fernandes' comments about United's history before he spoke was uncertain.

When asked again if he would take the captaincy away from the 32-year-old midfielder, Carrick repeated: "I will always do what is best for the football club."

He then refused to say whether he had spoken to Fernandes about his conduct, adding: "I don't think this is the time to go into too much detail."

Despite the challenge to his authority, Carrick said the United dressing room was not divided.

"No, it's not," he added. "We just need to get back to doing what we do best."

Carrick also said the club were 'doing everything' to support Fernandes and his family, whose Cheshire home was burgled on Wednesday.

"Thankfully they weren't directly affected even though it is an awful situation."

Carrick named legendary United figures such as Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney and Ferguson as examples of the humility, sacrifice and hard work expected of United players.

That was at odds with his post-match criticism on Wednesday, when he said if you don't run forward or back properly, you will not win games.

Asked how he would persuade his current squad to adhere to the values expected and he demanded, Carrick added: "It's clear as day.

"I'm not telling you anything new. I haven't invented that. That's the make-up of any good football team. You have to earn the right to be better than your opponent. That never changes.

"What we look like as a group is my responsibility. That's the privileged position I am in. I'll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and everyone else to stay dry.

"[Wednesday] hurts an awful lot, but that doesn't stop me. That hurt is used as pure motivation and inspiration to want more, expect more and get us going in a different direction."

#585. 7 Best Phones You Can’t Buy in the US (2026)

There’s a world of excellent phones—flagship smartphones that push photography to new levels, and budget buys that defy expectations—that you won’t find in the US for various reasons. Some Chinese phone manufacturers are banned domestically, while other brands prefer to focus their efforts in countries where Apple doesn’t have a massive market share. Whatever the explanation, I have a strong grasp of the best phones you can’t officially buy in the US, having tested global handsets for years.

Many of these phone manufacturers release multiple devices under sub-brands. With that in mind, here’s some basic information: Xiaomi is the brand behind Poco and Redmi; Nubia came from ZTE; Honor was a subsidiary of Huawei but separated after Huawei was banned in the US; and Realme spun out of Oppo. Folks in the UK and elsewhere in Europe can buy many of the phones in our guides to the Best Android Phones, Best iPhones, and Best Cheap Phones that are for sale in the US.

Updated October 2026: I added the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, Nothing Phone (4b), mentions of the TCL P80 Ultra, Xiaomi Poco F9 Ultra and Pro, and Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro Max, and removed some older devices.

There’s a new camera king in town. Oppo has gone all out on the photography front with the new Find X10 Pro Max, packing the first triple-lens 200-megapixel camera system into a phone. The three Samsung sensors deliver a seamless experience, from close-up macro photography to 3X optical zoom. (You can zoom in further without losing detail by cropping.) There’s more to a camera than a megapixel count, but the Hasselblad partnership ensures excellent tuning for precise color matching across lenses, and a range of shooting options that will satisfy pros. I’ve been impressed with the photos I’ve taken with this phone, and the balance of light, detail, and natural color is fantastic. Each camera can also shoot 4K video at 120 frames per second (8K/30 fps). If you crave an even more powerful zoom capability, check out the Teleconverter Kit for a special case and a long zoom lens to take optical zoom up to 10X and beyond (if you crop).

The build quality is excellent, the finish leans heavily into Hasselblad’s design language, and it scores an IP68/69 rating for durability. The silky-smooth 6.78-inch AMOLED display is bright and crisp, with a 144-Hz refresh rate. There’s a MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro processor inside, with 256 GB of speedy storage (UFS 4.1) and 12 GB of RAM in the base model. The 7,150-mAh battery may stretch to two days for casual users, and it supports 80-watt wired charging or 50-watt wireless charging with the right gear (, no Qi2 magnets). The highly customizable and slick ColorOS 17 sits atop Android 17, and my only real complaint (apart from the translucent aping of Apple) is the bumper crop of bloatware.

For fans of OnePlus, no longer operating in the US or Europe, parent company Oppo's flagship is as close as you’ll get now. If you can live with a smaller screen and a 50-MP ultrawide, the Oppo Find X10 (£1,099) is otherwise identical, but much cheaper.

The latest flagship sailing out of Xiaomi is the 17 Ultra (there was no 16), and she's a beauty. The now familiar design, with that huge circular camera module on the back, has ostensibly dropped a lens, but the main 50-megapixel shooter boasts a new 1-inch sensor and lens pairing that helped me capture stunning shots in a variety of scenarios. There’s just one telephoto lens on this edition, but it’s a 200-megapixel shooter that slides between 3.2X (75 mm) and 4.3X (100 mm) optical zoom. A 50-megapixel ultrawide and a 50-megapixel front-facing camera round out a truly top-notch camera system.

The rest of the phone ain’t bad either, with a flat 6.9-inch OLED display, speedy processor, and generous RAM and storage. You also get improved battery life and fast wired or wireless charging. I love the speckled green finish (regular black or white are options). Xiaomi has committed to four Android updates and six years of security patches, too. But no device is perfect, so you’ll have to deal with flaws like bloatware, Xiaomi’s HyperOS software, and that colossal camera bump. I also think Xiaomi’s AI features are slightly below par.

Last year, Xiaomi leaned into its partnership with Leica with the 15 Ultra, but it goes even further with the special edition Leitzphone (£1,699, about $2,252). If you don’t mind spending a chunk more, this retro-camera-style beauty adds Leica touches inside and out but retains everything that makes the Xiaomi 17 Ultra so good.

The first folding phone to win me over was the Honor Magic V3. The Magic V5 (there was no V4) was slightly better, and the Magic V6 is another incremental improvement that brings better battery life, faster charging, and greater durability in a very similar book-style foldable form (4.1 millimeters open, 8.8 mm closed), ignoring the sizable camera bump. There’s also an interesting new red-and-gold finish with a vegan leather back that you’ll love or hate (black, white, and gold are available for the less adventurous). It’s a pleasure to use and feels close to a regular phone when closed, but it has two lovely screens (6.52-inch and 7.95-inch), a versatile camera, and a responsive fingerprint sensor in the power button. Honor’s MagicOS software includes potentially useful foldable and AI features, though I could live without all the bloatware.

Fitting flagship cameras into folding phones is tough, so they usually end up with a big camera module that undermines the svelte design and catches on your pocket. Honor has managed to keep the same excellent camera system as the V5 but slimmed that bump a bit in the V6 (it’s still big, though). It captures lovely photos in most scenarios, though the cameras in the Xiaomi 17 Ultra and Honor Magic 8 Pro are both slightly better. But the V6 does feel like a flagship, and this is a phone with no obvious weaknesses. Battery life is excellent; it charges up very quickly, performance is smooth, and the software is mostly slick. If Honor sold it in the US, the V6 would be a serious contender for top place in our Best Folding Phones guide.

If you’re a mobile gaming purist, the Nubia Redmagic 11S Pro is for you. From the transparent industrial design with built-in fans and RGB lighting to the unbroken, almost bezel-free 6.85-inch AMOLED (active-matrix organic light-emitting diode) screen and 144-Hz refresh rate, this phone is built for gaming. You also get a whopping 7,500-mAh battery and customizable capacitive-touch shoulder triggers. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 ensures snappy performance (overclocked here) and is backed by speedy RAM (LPDDR5T) and storage (UFS 4.1 Pro). The 11S Pro can run all your favorite mobile games, cranked to the max. The cooling is highly effective, and there’s a dedicated game space and mode. It also supports Wi-Fi 7 and has a 3.5-mm headphone port (a rarity nowadays).

This iterative update to the 11 Pro—itself a slight update on the Redmagic 10S Pro, which was a slight update on the 10 Pro (you get the picture)—is almost indistinguishable from that previous model. This pointless mid-cycle update purports to offer improvements over the 11 Pro (overclocked processor, better cooling), but the only difference you’ll notice is the hefty price bump. It still wins the dedicated gaming phone category, but mostly because there's no competition. The camera still disappoints; the main 50-MP shooter is passable, but it’s paired with a 50-MP ultrawide (I’d prefer a telephoto) and a subpar underscreen selfie camera. The software is also shoddy in places.

While the 11S Pro boasts stunning performance for the price, the virtually unchanged clunky design, software, and subpar camera erode its bargain credentials, particularly if you’re not using it for gaming.

The impressively affordable Honor 600 is a tempting package that includes a crisp, bright AMOLED display, long battery life, top-notch water resistance, and a powerful main camera. The design is derivative; my review unit apes the orange iPhone 17 Pro with the same color and camera module. But it feels nice in hand and can survive a dunk in fresh water. The Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 processor is fast enough for most folks; I had no issues switching between apps or shooting up the opposition in Call of Duty: Mobile. The battery life is great (even if Honor did cut down the size compared with the Chinese version), and this phone is quick to charge when you plug it in (it lacks wireless charging). The main 200-megapixel camera is very good, and it enables a decent level of zoom through cropping. Honor includes a bunch of AI camera tricks in the software if you want to play around.

But for all its strengths, the Honor 600 is ultimately a mixed bag. Shortcomings include a weak 12-megapixel ultrawide, the sometimes overzealous AI that makes shots look unnatural, and the pernicious presence of bloatware. The 8 GB of RAM also feels stingy. But flaws aside, the reason the Honor 600 claims this spot is the price. At the time of writing, you can snag this at Amazon for less than £400 (about $533). If you want better performance and wireless charging, you can opt for the 600 Pro, but for a price of hundreds more, it’s not nearly as attractive.

In a sea of black glass rectangles, it’s nice to see something different. Nothing’s style, mixing industrial translucent design with bright colors and fun features like the customizable LED Glyph Bar, is fresh, even if it is a little watered down here compared to the Nothing Phone (4a) Pro. With prices climbing and sales dwindling, the budget end of the phone market is being squeezed, and there’s little choice at this price. The design, the 6.77-inch Super AMOLED screen, and the 5,200-mAh battery are highlights. You also get an IP64 rating, decent stereo speakers, and Nothing’s monochromatic retro pixel software skin. The Glyph bar can light up different colors and pulse to help you identify an alert or a specific contact, but it’s a bit gimmicky. The main 50-megapixel camera is fine for a phone at this price.

Inevitably, there are compromises in cheaper phones. The main one here is the Qualcomm Snapdragon 6 Gen 4 processor, paired with just 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. Everything is slower than a flagship phone. Games like Asphalt Legends are perfectly playable with the odd dropped frame, and I noticed some lag in the camera app, but nothing too annoying. Compared with pricier options, the Nothing Phone (4b) has larger bezels around a screen that doesn’t get as bright, lacks wireless charging, and has a pretty poor 8-megapixel ultrawide lens, with no telephoto for zoom. I was also disappointed to find a little bloatware. But this is the best option at this price right now.

Scoring a perfect 10 on iFixit's repairability scale is rare, but the Fairphone (Gen. 6) achieved it, making it a great pick if longevity is important to you. Fairphone also aims to be as environmentally friendly and ethical as possible, carefully sourcing components, using recycled materials wherever possible, and committing to decent wages and conditions. While previous Fairphone editions shared in that mission, those models often compromised on basic specs and had a dull design. The Fairphone (Gen 6) is different, with modular accessories, a clever distraction-free mode triggered by a dedicated switch, and a pretty decent camera system.

While the specs are respectable, you can find more powerful hardware in this guide for less money. The Fairphone also lacks wireless charging and only scores an IP55 rating for water resistance (which is fine for rain but don't submerge it). That said, ethical options are virtually nonexistent in the smartphone market, so the Fairphone is one of a kind in that sense. Good news for folks in the US: you can buy the newer Fairphone (Gen 6+).

Haven’t seen anything you like? The following phones are also worth considering:

TCL P80 Ultra for £480: I love that the 6.8-inch AMOLED screen transforms into an e-ink screen at the flick of a switch; it’s also wonderfully matte, even in AMOLED mode, which makes it more comfortable to read for hours than most phone screens. TCL has also packed in a versatile camera, including a decent telephoto lens, and solid battery life. But the plain design and occasional sluggishness make it a tough sell at this price. If reading is your main priority, the compromises may be worth it.

Xiaomi Poco F9 Ultra for £999 and F9 Pro for £799: This year's unfortunate price jump, combined with Xiaomi's weird pricing (low early-bird prices and frequent discounts, but very high MSRPs), makes these phones tough to recommend. Both are actually very good, with lovely displays, good battery life and performance, great stereo speakers, and versatile triple-lens cameras. Naturally, the Ultra is slightly bigger and better. Sadly, they signal a major departure from Poco’s budget roots, but if you see them discounted (I’ve seen the Ultra for £669 and the Pro for £579), they are worth considering.

Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro Max for £499: With a huge battery that easily lasts two days, a big screen, great build quality, and impressive durability, the Redmi Note 17 Pro Max makes a strong first impression. Performance is mediocre, the camera is limited, and it’s packed with bloatware. Unless battery life is your top priority, I’d pick something else.

Honor Magic 8 Pro for £894: This phone boasts excellent camera performance and AI assistance across the board, with a raft of refinements over Honor’s Magic 7 Pro. Its slimmed-down design with subtle curves makes it a pleasure to handle, and Honor has managed to pack in a much larger silicon-carbon battery. The versatile camera also zooms farther (3.7X optical zoom) and handles low light and shaky hands with aplomb (night photography is especially strong). That said, the image processing can be heavy-handed at times. The 6.71-inch screen is gorgeous, razor-sharp, and gets very bright. Honor’s Magic OS 10 is seriously slick on top of Android 16, and Honor AI genuinely adds value, from photo editing to contextual task handling; you can bring it to life with the dedicated AI button. There’s also support for Google Gemini, if you prefer. This is definitely not a phone for AI skeptics. Throw in secure face unlock, incredibly fast wired (100 watts) and wireless charging (80 watts) with the right gear, plus seven years of Android and security patch updates, and you get a supremely sophisticated smartphone with very few discernible weaknesses. But with its successor due to land shortly, you should only snag this right now if you can get a decent discount.

Xiaomi Poco X8 Pro for $390 (£479) and Poco X8 Pro Max for $510 (£599): If anything, a slight step down from the now-discontinued F7, the X8 sports a smaller 6.59-inch AMOLED screen, a MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra chipset, and 8 GB of RAM in the basic model. Performance is solid (though it’s worth noting I used a 12-GB RAM review unit). And the slightly smaller body is a touch easier to handle. You get a big 6,500-mAh battery with plenty of stamina, plus 100-watt charging that gets you back to full in under an hour. The main camera is a solid 50-MP shooter, though the 8-MP ultrawide and 20-MP front-facing cameras aren’t great. I like the mint green model, but it also comes in black or white. There’s still too much bloatware to deal with, and Xiaomi’s software is not my favorite, but you get decent support, including four Android versions and six years of security updates. There’s no wireless charging, but that’s par for the course in this bracket. Overall, the Poco X8 Pro is the best phone for its price. If battery life is a priority, consider the X8 Pro Max, which jumps up to 8,500 mAh. It also has a bigger screen, a better processor, and Wi-Fi 7 support.

Xiaomi 17T for £649 and 17T Pro for $780: Without Honor’s aggressively low pricing, one of these phones (probably the 17T) would have claimed the best mid-range spot above. Compared with the Honor 600, the 17T offers slightly better performance with more RAM and a more reliable camera that has superior zoom capability. Unfortunately, it also comes with a lot of bloatware, and the software needs some tinkering to get the best it offers. The 17T Pro adds wireless charging, a bigger battery, much better performance with a faster chipset, and a larger screen—but it’s even more expensive, pushing the top end of what I’d consider midrange.

Oppo Find N6 for $1,899: Touting an 8.12-inch display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its creaseless promise, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it with the screen on, but you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide, though it can’t quite compete with the Xiaomi 17 Ultra above. The global model supports familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import them, since the phone won’t officially launch in the West, which is why it can't edge out Honor’s foldable above.

Xiaomi 17 Pro Max for $1,129: The Xiaomi 17 Pro Max differs from the 17 Pro mainly with a refreshing design that adds a second, smaller screen on the back to house the camera lenses. Xiaomi offers several creative ways to use this auxiliary display, including a selfie preview for better main-camera selfies, music controls, customizable themes, and virtual pets. There’s even a retro gaming case that lets you play Angry Birds, though it feels a bit silly when there’s a 6.7-inch screen on the other side. Aside from the second screen, the 17 Pro Max is a typical Xiaomi specs beast, and the 17 Pro isn’t far behind, but neither has been officially released outside China yet.

Oppo Find X9 Pro for £1,099: Photography fans simply must check out the Oppo Find X9 Pro. The 200-megapixel telephoto lens supports 3X optical zoom and can take excellent shots at 6X zoom by cropping images down to 50 megapixels. To maximize camera capabilities, though, you’ll need the detachable Hasselblad Teleconverter Kit ($400). This enormous lens slots into place on the case and adds another 3.28X zoom, though it’s tricky to use without a tripod. An additional trio of 50-MP lenses, with all supporting 4K video recording at 60 fps with HDR, makes this a great pick for creatives. Impressive specs include a 6.78-inch flat display, IP66/68/69 ratings, and a 7,500-mAh silicon-carbon battery that’ll last for two days.

Xiaomi Poco F8 Ultra for £649 and F8 Pro for £406: Xiaomi’s cheaper, youthful brand Poco provides room for experimentation, but the company’s own 15T Pro is a better buy in this price bracket. What the F8 Ultra offers that you won’t find elsewhere is a fun (or awful, depending on your tastes) denim finish on the back. There are also Bose-tuned speakers, an excellent 6.9-inch display, and an enormous 6,500-mAh battery. It also has a flagship-level Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and generous RAM and storage. There’s even a trio of 50-MP lenses in the camera. The F8 Pro is slightly smaller but has similar specs, making it the better bargain.

Honor Magic 7 Pro for $985: Honor’s Magic 7 Pro features a solid triple-lens camera, a gorgeous 6.8-inch screen, speedy performance, good battery life, and dual IP68 and IP69 dust- and water-resistance ratings. Honor’s Magic OS boasts polished AI features, and Honor announced an increased commitment to seven years of Android version and security patch updates with this phone. The Magic 7 Pro’s downsides include its large camera cutout on the front, camera processing that’s sometimes heavy-handed, and an ultrawide camera that struggles to match the other two lenses.

Doro Aurora A20 for £250: Doro is a Swedish company focused on providing devices that are accessible for older folks. It primarily offers phones but also sells a decent video doorbell. The Aurora A20 is an odd spin on the flip phone that may help some people transition to a touchscreen device. It’s like an old candy bar HTC Android phone with a flip-out keypad attached to the bottom. There are lots of thoughtful features, including an alarm button, a spacious keypad, and simplified software. It’s also fairly cheap, but I found the performance sluggish, the camera poor, and the design a bit chunky and heavy.

Realme 14 Pro+ for €369: The color-changing finish may be gimmicky, but it's fun, and this phone looks and feels far more expensive than it is. There are more highs than lows on the spec sheet: You get a triple-lens camera, an IP68/69 water-resistance rating, a 6,000-mAh battery, and a 6.83-inch OLED display with a 120-Hz refresh rate. But the Snapdragon 7s Gen 3 chipset is limited, there's no wireless charging support, and you don’t get a charger in the box. Even so, it’s still quite a bargain.

Xiaomi 15 for $690: Folks seeking a compact phone could do a lot worse than the Xiaomi 15. It feels lovely and has a 6.36-inch screen, a decent triple-lens camera, and top-notch internals. But it’s a conservative design, and it has software and bloatware issues.

Honor Magic 7 RSR for £1,550: Designed with Porsche, this souped-up version of the 7 Pro above has a fancier design with a hexagonal camera module, a slightly improved telephoto lens, 24 GB of RAM, 1 TB of storage, and a bigger battery (5,850 mAh). It’s lovely, but it doesn’t justify the extra cost.

These aren’t necessarily bad phones, but I think you’d be better served by an option above.

Nothing Phone (3a) Lite: Nothing’s translucent hardware and pixelated software give it a retro-cool vibe, and it is currently the cheapest phone it offers in the UK (it wasn’t released in the US). The screen, battery life, and software are decent, but the camera and bloatware were disappointing. I don’t think the Nothing Phone (3a) Lite is the worst, but you can do better.

Nubia Z80 Ultra: Like my gaming pick above, the Nubia Redmagic 11S Pro, the Nubia Z80 Ultra trades a better camera for slightly lower performance and screen quality. It’s also a real brick, with an enormous camera module on the back that makes it awkward to handle, though I do like the dedicated camera button. Despite a very impressive spec sheet for the money, it manages to feel like less than the sum of its parts. Nubia’s software is subpar, and for this phone, it commits to only three years of security updates and a single Android version upgrade.

Oppo Reno 13 Pro 5G: This slim, lightweight midrange phone boasts a 6.8-inch screen (brightness is limited), a triple-lens camera (solid 50-MP main and telephoto lenses with a disappointing 8-MP ultrawide), and an impressive IP69 water-resistance rating. Battery life is good, and wired charging is fast, but there’s no wireless charging. It’s packed with bloatware, but it also adds AI features and tools for transcription, summarization, image editing, and more that may add value for some folks. After some time with the 13 Pro, I feel you can do better for the money.

Xiaomi Mix Fold 4: Officially released only in China, the Xiaomi Mix Fold 4 is a stylish folding phone with a 6.56-inch outer screen that folds open to reveal a 7.98-inch inner screen. It also offers solid performance and battery life, but despite having a large quad-lens camera module, the camera is underwhelming. The crease is also pronounced, and using a Chinese model is a bit of a pain, as various items are not translated and getting the apps you want takes work.

Realme GT7 Pro: This potential flagship killer has a 6.78-inch OLED screen, a Snapdragon 8 Elite chip, and an enormous 6,500-mAh battery. You also get a triple-lens camera, but the 50-megapixel main and telephoto lenses are let down by the 8-megapixel ultrawide. It also lacks wireless charging, and it only seems to be for sale in Germany.

Xiaomi Redmi Note 14 Pro+: Here, you get an attractive, durable design (IP68), a 200-megapixel Samsung camera sensor, and decent battery life with superfast charging (120 watts). But those wins come at the price of middling performance, poor ultrawide (8 MP) and macro (2 MP) lenses, and a ton of bloatware. Ultimately, there’s little improvement over last year’s Redmi Note 13 Pro+. Not only are there better phones for the same money, but there are also better Xiaomi phones.

While some phones are not officially sold in the US (or certain other countries), you can still get your hands on them if you’d like. They're often easy to buy online, and you may even find some on Amazon, often via third-party sellers. But before you buy, you’ll want to consider a few factors.

The technologies and specific bands upon which cellular networks rely differ from country to country. While models described as “global” and even specifically UK or European models are likely to work in the US, they may not support all the bands your carrier uses. Missing LTE or 5G bands can mean patchy service or even relegate you to 3G. Chinese and other country-specific models will almost certainly lack some common US bands and may not work on some carrier networks.

You will often find this information in the listing or aggregated on websites like Kimovil, but I recommend checking directly with the manufacturer and your carrier.

Depending on where you buy, importing a phone can lead to customs charges and add a significant expense to the overall cost. Do your research and factor in any extra fees before you buy.

It is common for phones released only in China to ship without any Google services, including the Google Play Store. Many Chinese manufacturers have their own app stores or preinstall third-party app stores for the Chinese market. Sometimes it's a simple case of checking a box to unlock and download Google services, but it’s not always so easy.

Even where Google services are supported, some Chinese phones won’t work properly with certain apps, such as Android Auto. Lack of support can leave you stuck with specific Chinese default apps and services, and many banking apps won’t work as they would on a US or global model.

With regard to Huawei phones in particular, the company developed an independent ecosystem of apps and services following its US ban. The latest models run HarmonyOS. Although it was originally forked from the Android Open Source Project, it is now completely separate, and Huawei phones can no longer run Android apps.

I try to use every smartphone I test as my main phone for at least a week, sometimes longer. I stress-test performance by playing the most demanding mobile games and recording videos at the highest resolution. I make calls to test the smartphone's microphone and speaker quality.

I often test the camera side by side with a competing phone and analyze the photos on a larger, more color-accurate screen. I've been reviewing all kinds of smartphones, from budget devices to flagships, for more than a decade.

#587. The Bundestag has debated the genocide Germany carried out in Namibia a century ago. But will it spur progress on addressing colonial crimes?

Opposition parties have forced a debate in the Bundestag on the early-20th-century genocide Germany carried out in Namibia. Will this finally spur progress in addressing colonial crimes?

Gaob Daniel Timotheus Frederick was sitting in the front row of the visitors' gallery in the Bundestag this week. Wearing a suit and hat, he had traveled all the way from Namibia to see this parliamentary debate unfold. For almost 120 years, his family had been waiting for the return of human remains of their ancestor, Cornelius Frederick (sometimes spelled Fredericks), who had led the Nama resistance against German colonial rule and died on Shark Island in Germany's first concentration camp.

In the name of his great-grandfather and as a member of the Nama Traditional Leaders Association (NTLA), Frederick was there to demand an "unconditioned apology" from Germany.

Sitting next to him, in uniform and white gloves, with a carved lion on the handle of his walking stick, was the head of the Ovaherero Traditional Authority, Paramount Chief Mutjinde Katjiua. Speaking before the Bundestag debate, the chief said: "We call upon the Bundestag to recognize unequivocally the genocides committed against the Ovaherero and Nama peoples."

Many people wonder why the German parliament hasn't already done this — and why the government has not yet issued an official apology. There is a draft joint declaration with Namibia in which the German government acknowledges that "from today's perspective, [it] would be called genocide." But there is no German-Namibian reconciliation agreement. The evidence is overwhelming: From 1904 to 1908, the German Empire waged a war of extermination against the Indigenous people of southwestern Africa, including the Ovaherero (also known as the Herero), the Nama, the Damara and the San. At least 100,000 people were killed, and just as many displaced. Many were subjected to forced labor and forced prostitution. The land seizures and expropriation carried out at the time continue to affect their descendants today.

Jürgen Zimmerer, a professor of history at the University of Hamburg whose research focuses on Africa, told DW that the Bundestag and government lack the will to confront this era in German history. "There are Bundestag resolutions on the Armenian genocide, one on the Holodomor [in Ukraine], and one on the genocide against the Yazidis [by the "Islamic State" in Iraq]. But there is no recognition of the genocide against the Herero and Nama by the German Bundestag." If there were any political will to do so, Zimmerer said, it could happen very quickly.

The socialist Left Party initiated the Bundestag debate by drafting a resolution calling for full recognition and compensation in collaboration with representatives of the descendants. The goal: "restorative justice." Paramount Chief Katjiua has rejected the existing agreement between the Namibian and German governments. "Development aid cannot substitute for comprehensive reparations," he said.

Since 2021, the governments have been negotiating a joint declaration that pledges €1.1 billion ($1.24 billion) in reconstruction aid to Namibia over 30 years. Once the agreement is signed, Germany's president is set to issue a formal apology.

But the Foreign Ministry warned: "Legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from the recognition of genocide. With these negotiations — which are unique worldwide — Namibia and Germany have broken new ground and are pioneers in confronting their colonial past."

Political scientist Andreas Mehler, the director of the Anton Bergstraesser Institute at the University of Freiburg, said the government's plan sounded like "checkbook diplomacy."

Zimmerer also said there was a financial calculation: "If we were to recognize an obligation to provide reparations to the families of those killed — given the millions of victims of World War II, the victims of the Germans — it would ruin us."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Four lines in the 144 pages of the coalition agreement of the current German government — between the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — summarize the extent of the government's commitment to reconciliation with Namibia.

"We will intensify our efforts to come to terms with colonialism," the text reads. "This includes transnational research into artifacts and the restitution of cultural property in dialogue with the countries of origin. Particular attention will be paid to establishing a dignified memorial site and the repatriation of human remains."

Compared with the efforts to address colonialism led by the SPD-led government from 2021 to 2025, "the issue has lost visibility," said Alexander Stroh-Steckelberg, a professor of political scientist at the University of Bayreuth who specializes in Africa.

Zimmerer has an even more critical take: "I wouldn't even call it a stalemate anymore. I believe this government is rolling back the progress that has been made in terms of raising awareness of colonial injustices."

Much remains to be done, as far the descendants of the Ovaherero are concerned: The remains of tens of thousands of people are believed to still be in Germany. Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick and other descendants of the victims have been fighting to heal these wounds for generations.

In March, Germany established a coordination council, headed by the Foreign Ministry, which stated that the government did not wish to "dictate to the countries and societies of origin which cultural artifacts and human remains they should reclaim, what priorities they should set or how restitutions should be handled."

Serap Güler, a state minister in the Foreign Ministry and the chair of the coordination council, defends the government's actions so far. Recounting her own official trips — she has already been to Togo, and next week she plans to travel to Rwanda and Burundi — she said: "Everywhere I go, I receive recognition for our sincere and trusting approach to the past — as well as for our determined commitment to a future of freedom, security and prosperity."

Zimmerer said Germany "has earned a reputation as a country that takes a critical view of its own history and learns from its mistakes" — which gives it "enormous cultural capital" on the world stage. But he is concerned that this capital is currently being squandered.

The government's memorial policy does not appear to address colonialism. Zimmerer even detects an attempt to "marginalize German colonial crimes" in the recent proposal by Minister of State for Culture Wolfram Weimer to create a dignified memorial site in Bremen. He notes that victim groups have not been included in Weimer's proposal and said the colonial capitals of the German Empire — Berlin and Hamburg — must also become sites of remembrance.

Ninety-five percent of the colonial troops set sail from Hamburg's Baakenhafen, including Commander Lothar von Trotha, who issued the orders to exterminate the Ovaherero and Nama. According to Zimmerer, the fact that a new opera house — rather than a memorial site — is being built at Baakenhafen constitutes a staggering case of "art-washing of history." Mehler also hopes that a productive debate on memorial sites will still take place and that, overall, "many more places will come to terms with colonial history."

Meanwhile, Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick continues to call for a collective effort to come to terms with the past: "Let us give opportunity to the affected communities that are being represented by us to have a seat on the table to discuss with them the rest of the way."

This article was originally written in German.

The legendary RPG studio behind classics such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect, and Dragon Age is no more.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The writing was on the wall, but the news still hit us like a truck yesterday. BioWare, the iconic RPG studio behind the Mass Effect and Dragon Age series, is no more. Development on the next Mass Effect has stopped, but EA might not be entirely done with the IP.

Variety reported, backed by EA’s own statement and BioWare’s goodbye on socials, that EA is laying off 3% of its global workforce and closing down BioWare. The shift comes shortly after the company went fully private this summer, with Saudi Arabia and private equity acquiring it alongside all its studios and properties.

A new Mass Effect game — meant to serve as a follow-up to the original trilogy — had been in development since the early 2020s, though progress was slow following severe downsizing after 2024’s Dragon Age: The Veilguard failed to meet EA’s expectations. According to Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier, only around 50 staff remained at the studio, which would’ve needed to go on a hiring spree to complete development of the massive sci-fi RPG.

The first post-shutdown shocker arrived a bit later, with IGN exclusively revealing that Mass Effect isn't entirely dead, as the upcoming live-action TV show based on Mass Effect is still moving forward at Prime Video.

The series started active development at Amazon in late 2024, but it has yet to reach production status. Little is known about the story, but rumors point to it aiming to bridge the gap between the original trilogy and the now-cancelled new game. Despite closing the studio that created it, EA still owns the Mass Effect property.

Variety’s report, which includes more comments from EA’s top brass about the present and future of the publisher, also contains updates on Marvel’s Iron Man (developed at Motive) and Star Wars Jedi 3 (Respawn Entertainment). Both are still coming, and the more surprising news comes in the shape of DICE and Respawn teaming up for a totally new project, believed to be Star Wars Battlefront 3 after days of strong rumors from a number of reputable sources.

Elsewhere, ex-BioWare developers have teamed up at new studios like Archetype and Arcanaut. The former is preparing to ship Mass Effect-inspired action RPG Exodus in 2027, and the latter recently started work on Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic, with original Knights of the Old Republic (and Mass Effect) director Casey Hudson behind the wheel.

Here’s hoping both studios, as well as the recently laid-off developers, can find success in an increasingly hostile industry.
